The end of Umaro Sissoco Embaló's disputed term has left a relative political vacuum, marked by debates over the legitimacy of the new authorities and over the timetable for a return to constitutional order. In the streets of Bissau, as in the rest of the country, this uncertainty translates into widespread caution: slowed-down administrations, deferred economic decisions, and political actors waiting for clear signals.

A fragile economy, purchasing power under pressure

Economically, the effects of the transition are being felt. Heavily dependent on cashew nut exports, Guinea-Bissau remains vulnerable to political shocks. Business operators fear a slowdown in activity, while households face a high cost of living, particularly for imported goods.

The informal sector, which employs a large share of the population, nevertheless continues to act as a social shock absorber. Markets remain lively, a sign of a survival economy that adapts, even in the absence of clear short-term prospects.

Public services and social expectations

In health and education, the situation remains mixed. While essential services are functioning, they suffer from a chronic lack of resources, made worse by political instability. Trade unions are calling for guarantees on the regular payment of salaries and the continuity of social policies, fearing that the transition will push these priorities onto the back burner.

For young people, who make up the majority of the population, the post-Embaló era is seen as both a source of hope and of frustration. Many aspire to more inclusive governance and economic opportunities, but fear a prolonged transition that would delay these promises yet again.

Between weariness and hope for renewal

Socially, the former president's removal has revived debates over governance, corruption and the place of the army in political life. While some welcome the end of a rule deemed authoritarian, others fear a new episode of instability, recalling the many precedents of aborted transitions in the country's history.

Even so, part of civil society sees this period as a turning point, one that could pave the way for a national dialogue and a rebuilding of institutions.

A future that hangs on political choices

Life for Bissau-Guineans after the removal of Umaro Sissoco Embaló is thus defined by a fragile balance between the continuity of everyday life and political uncertainty. More than changes in leadership, the population now expects concrete action: stability, functioning public services and economic prospects.

In a country where normality has often been the exception, the challenge for the new authorities is clear: to turn this transition into an opportunity for a positive break with the past, so that the post-Embaló era is not just one more parenthesis, but the starting point of lasting stability.

Writer: BAWA ALLAH Khadidjatou A.
en.4596:
Gitega, 8 December 2025 (PRESS AFRICA) In recent years, Burundi has shown notable progress in its economy, the management of its public finances and the development of its road infrastructure. This progress reflects a strong commitment by the Burundian authorities, supported by international financial partners, to consolidate growth and improve the quality of life of the population.

Financial reforms under way

Strengthening public financial management is one of the pillars of Burundi's economic transformation. In January 2024, the World Bank approved US$42 million in support to modernize the state's financial systems, notably through the digitization of public services and the integration of expenditure management platforms.

According to the World Bank's Country Economic Memorandum, Burundi has considerable potential in the agricultural and trade sectors. The authorities have begun reforms aimed at stimulating private investment, strengthening the competitiveness of agricultural value chains and diversifying the economy. These efforts are part of the "Burundi 2025" vision, which provides for an improved business climate, a review of commercial codes and greater involvement of the private sector through public-private partnerships.

Expanding road infrastructure

On infrastructure, Burundi benefits from substantial World Bank support to strengthen road connectivity in strategic areas. The Transport Resilience Project, financed to the tune of US$120 million by the IDA, aims to rehabilitate key road sections, in particular the vital corridor linking Burundi to Tanzania, while incorporating climate resilience measures.

In addition, in its 2024-2029 strategy, the African Development Bank (AfDB) plans to support the construction and modernization of multimodal transport infrastructure, including a 45-kilometer cross-border road.

Toward inclusive and resilient growth

These road investments are not purely technical: they are designed to strengthen access to markets, facilitate trade and energize the rural economy. The World Bank-backed transport project also includes social components, such as safe infrastructure for vulnerable users.

Likewise, the AfDB's strategy emphasizes "green and inclusive" growth, combining transport development, renewable energy and economic governance.

A record judged satisfactory, but challenges remain

During the May 2025 portfolio review, the Burundian authorities and the AfDB welcomed the overall performance of the projects, while acknowledging persistent obstacles including administrative delays, the late start of some programs and the need to strengthen local capacity.

These challenges show that, despite encouraging results, fully realizing Burundi's development vision will require rigorous implementation and sustained cooperation with donors.

Burundi now appears to be on a stronger trajectory. Thanks to ambitious financial reforms, significant international support and targeted investment in road infrastructure, the country is increasing its macroeconomic resilience. If these efforts continue, they could lay the foundations for more inclusive, sustainable growth, firmly anchored in modernized governance.

Writer: BAWA ALLAH Khadidjatou A.
en.4587:
Yaoundé, 8 December 2025—PRESS AFRICA—Cameroon continues to occupy a strategic place in Africa, positioning itself as an important development player but one facing major structural challenges. At continental level, its development ranking reflects this duality: undeniable progress in some sectors, but persistent weaknesses that hold back its transformation.

Moderate performance at continental level

With a diversified economy — agriculture, industry, services — Cameroon stands out in the CEMAC sub-region. According to French Treasury indicators, it accounts for nearly 43% of CEMAC's GDP, making it an economic pivot of the zone.

In industry, it ranks 24th out of 52 African countries on the African Development Bank's (AfDB) Africa Industrialization Index (AII). This modest position reflects progress, but also the scale of the gap that remains to be closed with the continent's most industrialised nations.

Infrastructure challenges and weak structural capacity

According to an AfDB report, Cameroon suffers from a significant infrastructure deficit: it was ranked 28th out of 54 African countries on the Africa Infrastructure Development Index (AIDI), with a very low score, and its motorway ambitions are far from being met.

In the digital sector, the country is also slipping back: according to the ITU, it ranks 6th in Central Africa for ICT but has lost several places since 2017. Its digital strategy is ambitious — aiming to roll out broadband internet, connect rural areas and develop the digital industry — but results remain limited so far.

Economic growth, but inclusion still limited

According to the World Bank, Cameroon's growth was 3.5% in 2024, slightly up on the previous year, driven by agricultural sectors (cocoa, cotton) and a better electricity supply. Nevertheless, this growth remains insufficient to meet the ambitions of the country's National Development Strategy, and poverty remains high, with nearly 40% of the population below the national poverty line, according to the same institution.

The African Development Bank, in its 2025 Country Report, also calls on Yaoundé to mobilise domestic resources better in order to finance more inclusive development.

The lack of transparency

The World Bank's July 2025 report highlights the strategic role of Cameroon's forests — a veritable "green gold" — in the country's future growth. However, its membership of the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI) was suspended in 2024, which raises legitimate questions about the governance of revenue from natural resources.

Real strengths, but a difficult course to hold

Cameroon has undeniable development potential: a diversified economy, forest resources and a proactive digital strategy. At continental level, its ranking is not among the most advanced, but it remains a key player in Central Africa and beyond.

To step up, the country must remove its structural bottlenecks: improve its infrastructure, strengthen governance and mobilise its domestic resources transparently. If these levers are used effectively, Cameroon could not only consolidate its regional position but also climb the rankings of development in Africa — and contribute lastingly to more integrated African development.

Writer: BAWA ALLAH Khadidjatou A.
en.4586:
Bangui, 8 December 2025—PRESS AFRICA—The Central African Republic (CAR) remains in the grip of a deep social crisis in 2025, but some initiatives bring a glimmer of hope in a highly fragile context. Between poverty, food insecurity, population displacement and international support, the social impact on the lives of Central Africans is massive and multifaceted.

According to World Bank data, about 71% of the population lives in extreme poverty, combining monetary and non-monetary deprivation, including insufficient access to sanitation (69.9%) and electricity (87.7%). The humanitarian situation is worsened by mass displacement: as early as January 2025, there were more than 436,000 internally displaced people as well as around 680,000 refugees or asylum seekers.

Food insecurity remains a major challenge. The World Food Programme (WFP) warns that in 2025, 2.3 million Central Africans (35% of the population) could face acute food insecurity, including 431,000 people in emergency (IPC Phase 4) without a boost in aid.

In response, the WFP is advocating long-term initiatives: distribution of agricultural assets, strengthening of water and hygiene systems, social safety nets and school canteens to stabilise vulnerable families. Children's health and nutrition are particularly alarming: according to UNICEF's report, 38% of children under five suffer from chronic malnutrition, a factor that seriously compromises their development.

The maternal mortality rate (835 per 100,000 live births) and the under-five mortality rate (116 per 1,000) are among the highest in the world. This vulnerability is compounded by an extremely limited health system: according to one analysis, there are fewer than 0.05 doctors per 1,000 inhabitants, while many health centres are closed or destroyed.

Faced with these challenges, reinforcements are being provided through international aid: the World Bank has released a $30 million grant for an adaptive social safety nets project in the CAR, targeting around 45,000 vulnerable households in very poor rural regions.

In addition, a $70 million grant supports the PROVIR project ("inclusive and resilient cities"), aimed at improving access to basic services in urban areas exposed to climate hazards, notably Bangui and Berbérati, while also assisting internally displaced people, women and young people.

On the strategic front, the National Development Plan (PND) 2024-2028, adopted in June 2025, aims to strengthen human development, diversify the economy and improve governance, building on lessons learned from earlier peacebuilding phases.

Despite these efforts, structural challenges persist: the country remains heavily dependent on external aid (nearly 40% of the national budget comes from international aid according to some analyses), and social protection mechanisms are still embryonic.

The social impact in the CAR in 2025 is characterised by a constant tension between the severity of needs and the gradual rise of structural solutions. Humanitarian aid remains vital today, while investments in resilience, social protection and human development offer a measured but tangible hope to Central Africans.

Reporter: BAWA ALLAH Khadidjatou A.
en.4585:
Malabo, 8 December 2025 – PRESS AFRICA – In 2025, Equatorial Guinea faces a persistent challenge: the fight against tax evasion, a phenomenon deeply rooted in an economic system dependent on hydrocarbons and marked by still-opaque financial governance. As the country seeks to diversify its economy and improve budget transparency, tax evasion appears to be one of the main obstacles to mobilising the domestic resources essential for development.

Considerable lost revenue for the state

Equatorial Guinea, rich in oil and gas, has long enjoyed high revenues from the extractive sector. However, fluctuations in international prices and the gradual decline in production highlight more than ever the need to strengthen tax collection. In 2025, several regional economic reports point out that the country loses a significant share of its potential revenue every year, notably through the under-reporting of commercial activity, the illicit transfer of profits and evasion practices linked to companies operating in the energy sector.

Emerging sectors, such as telecommunications, import-export, construction and maritime services, are also affected by informal tax practices, encouraged by a still-weak digital system and a tax administration facing a capacity shortfall.

Reforms announced, but…

Faced with these challenges, the Equatorial Guinean authorities have announced several measures aimed at modernising the tax system: the gradual digitalisation of procedures, tighter customs controls, and a review of certain tax breaks deemed too lenient. In 2025, the government says it wants to further align its standards with those of CEMAC, which is working to reduce illicit financial flows in the region.

However, the implementation of these reforms still runs up against structural limits: a lack of technical resources, administrative opacity, a proliferation of exemptions, obstacles to access to information and the absence of independent external oversight. The lack of transparency in the management of state-owned enterprises is also a major brake.

The central role of governance and transparency

For several African economic analysts, the fight against tax evasion in Equatorial Guinea necessarily requires stronger governance. The absence of regular publication of public accounts, the country's weak participation in international transparency mechanisms and the marginalisation of civil society limit the room for progress.

The country's suspension from certain international transparency initiatives in the extractive industries has also fuelled criticism over a lack of political will to establish more open management of public finances.

A major issue for development

Tax evasion is today one of the most strategic challenges for Equatorial Guinea. At a time when oil resources are running out of steam and social needs (youth employment, infrastructure, health, education) are growing, the state's ability to mobilise domestic revenue is becoming a crucial pillar for financing sustainable development.

If the reforms launched in 2025 take hold and political will strengthens, Equatorial Guinea could gradually curb tax evasion and build a more transparent economic framework, better suited to its future transformation.

Writer: BAWA ALLAH Khadidjatou A.
en.4575:
Brazzaville, 8 December 2025 (PRESS AFRICA) Congo's cultural economy is establishing itself as a strategic sector at the heart of national ambitions for economic diversification in 2025. Long relegated to a secondary role behind hydrocarbons, the cultural sector is now emerging as an engine of growth, innovation and diplomatic influence, driven by a creative youth and a political will to showcase the national heritage.

A sector taking shape

Since 2023, the Congolese government has launched several reforms to structure the creative industries. In 2025, these efforts are reflected in the consolidation of the Arts and Culture Development Fund, the gradual professionalization of those working in the sector and the introduction of new standards governing audiovisual production, copyright and intellectual property. The goal: to make culture a fully integrated economic sector, capable of generating revenue, jobs and international appeal.

Private cultural organizations and artists' associations also play an important role in the ecosystem, particularly in music, independent film, fashion and the visual arts. In Brazzaville as in Pointe-Noire, studios and galleries are multiplying, training a new generation of creators connected to African and global trends.

Music and audiovisual: promising sectors

Congolese music, already renowned across the continent, is seeing the rise of new digital distribution platforms in 2025, encouraging artists to produce and market their work independently. Ndombolo and Congolese rumba are benefiting from greater visibility thanks to social media, while young talents are standing out in urban styles, spurred by regional collaborations with Central Africa, West Africa and the diaspora.

Film and audiovisual are also enjoying renewed energy, driven by training initiatives, local festivals and the arrival of new private players. Congolese filmmakers are exploring contemporary social themes and attracting growing interest from African festivals, which helps strengthen the country's cultural identity on the international stage.

Arts, heritage and cultural tourism

At the same time, the promotion of tangible and intangible heritage is a major pillar of the cultural economy. Historic sites, museums and art centers are attracting more visitors, while renovation projects are under way thanks to international partnerships. Cultural tourism, though still developing, is seen as an opportunity to diversify the economy and create new jobs.

A sector still fragile but promising

Despite this progress, the Congolese cultural sector still faces challenges: insufficient funding, limited infrastructure, persistent informality and restricted access to technology. Nevertheless, the dynamics of 2025 show a clear trend: culture is becoming an emerging economic pillar, a space for inventiveness and a strategic tool for Congo's diversification and influence.

Writer: BAWA ALLAH Khadidjatou A.
en.4574:
Kinshasa, 8 December 2025—PRESS AFRICA—Several companies in the Democratic Republic of Congo stand out in 2025 for their economic weight, strategic role and contribution to national development. From mining giants to public utilities, here is an overview of the ten most influential companies in the country.

Gécamines: the Générale des Carrières et des Mines (Gécamines) remains the country's leading state-owned mining company. Founded in Lubumbashi, it is active in the extraction of copper and cobalt, resources that are strategic for the energy transition.

Tenke Fungurume Mining (TFM): a major joint venture in copper and cobalt extraction, TFM is one of the country's biggest producers. It plays a central role in mining development.

Rawbank: the DRC's largest universal bank, Rawbank provides financial services to businesses, SMEs and individuals. It facilitates local investment and plays a key role in Congolese finance.

Bralima: a brewing subsidiary of Heineken, Bralima produces alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks in several Congolese cities such as Kinshasa, Kisangani and Lubumbashi. Its long history makes it a pillar of local industry.

SNEL (Société Nationale d'Électricité): the state-owned company responsible for the generation, transmission and distribution of electricity in the DRC. In 2025, it is engaged in a vast modernisation and recruitment plan to improve national electricity coverage.

Cohydro: a state-owned hydrocarbons company, Cohydro plays a central role in the import, distribution and trade of fuels across Congolese territory.

MIBA (Société Minière de Bakwanga): a historic player in the DRC's diamond industry, MIBA remains an important company despite structural challenges in the mining sector.

OKIMO (Office des Mines d'Or de Kilo-Moto): a state-owned company specialising in gold, OKIMO holds major concessions in the north-east of the DRC and plays a strategic role in gold mining.

SODIMICO (Société de Développement Industriel et Minier au Congo): a state-owned mining company, SODIMICO is among the Congolese state's holdings in several mining companies.

SNCC (Société Nationale des Chemins de Fer du Congo): a key player in rail transport, SNCC, a state-owned company, plays an essential role in domestic logistics and the transport of mineral resources, a vital link for the national economy.

Outlook…

These ten companies illustrate the diversity of the Congolese economic fabric: a dominant mining sector, but also state-owned companies in energy and transport infrastructure. They represent both levers of development and significant challenges: modernisation, governance and investment capacity.

Governance and transparency: several of these state-owned companies (such as Gécamines, SNEL and OKIMO) face governance challenges. Strengthening transparency and reducing debt are major issues.

Investment in infrastructure: SNEL in particular is carrying out an ambitious project to expand the power grid and bring electricity to rural areas, which could support industrial growth.

Strategic resources: miners such as TFM and Gécamines are at the heart of the global race for strategic metals (copper, cobalt), which gives the DRC a central role in the energy transition.

The DRC's corporate landscape in 2025 is marked by a mix of historic public players, international joint ventures and fast-growing banks. Their collective success is crucial to the country's economic development, and their institutional strengthening could make the Democratic Republic of Congo an even more influential player on the global economic stage.

Writer: BAWA ALLAH Khadidjatou A.
en.4573:
São Tomé, 8 December 2025—PRESS AFRICA—In 2025, São Tomé and Príncipe, a small Central African archipelago known for its relative stability, faces a series of sensitive issues that are shaping its public debate and political direction. Despite its modest size, the country is confronted with strategic challenges touching on governance, the economy, maritime security and the management of its natural resources.

Governance and institutional reform

Consolidating governance remains one of the most delicate issues. Debates over public transparency, the fight against corruption and the strengthening of institutions regularly return to the political arena. In 2025, citizens' expectations are becoming pressing in the face of slow administrative reforms and the challenge of stabilising relations between the executive and legislative branches. Civil society organisations are calling for more oversight mechanisms and citizen participation in the running of the state.

An economy under strain and structural dependence

Economically, São Tomé and Príncipe continues to depend heavily on external aid, cocoa and services. This vulnerability is a sensitive issue, especially in a context of budgetary pressure. Reforms to diversify the economy, notably towards sustainable tourism, modernised fishing and renewable energy, are moving forward but remain hampered by a lack of structural investment and limited infrastructure. Public debt and control of government spending feed political discussions.

Hydrocarbons: hopes, delays and controversy

The management of the joint oil exploration zone with Nigeria continues to raise expectations and questions. Although oil prospects have been announced for more than a decade, concrete results are slow to materialise. This uncertainty creates a climate of social frustration and fuels debate over transparency in energy agreements, foreign partnerships and financial projections. The oil question thus remains a symbol of the tension between hopes of prosperity and economic caution.

Maritime security and cross-border crime

In 2025, maritime security is among the most sensitive issues, in particular because of the country's strategic position in the Gulf of Guinea. Piracy, illegal fishing and cross-border trafficking are forcing the archipelago to strengthen its surveillance capabilities and to work more closely with regional powers. Although the situation is relatively under control, maritime vulnerability remains a national concern.

Social pressures and environmental concerns

Social issues — the cost of living, youth unemployment, the quality of public services — remain at the heart of people's demands. At the same time, environmental challenges, notably coastal erosion, deforestation and the protection of biodiversity, have become sensitive priorities in a country highly exposed to the effects of climate change. Environmental campaigners are calling for more rigorous policies to preserve the archipelago.

In 2025, São Tomé and Príncipe therefore stands at the crossroads of several crucial issues. While they represent real challenges, these matters are also opportunities to redefine the country's development and to strengthen the resilience of an island state in the midst of change.

Reporter: BAWA ALLAH Khadidjatou A.
en.4572:
Mogadishu, 8 December 2025 – PRESS AFRICA – In Somalia, people's daily lives are a mix of persistent challenges, coping strategies and remarkable resilience. In 2025, despite a gradual improvement in the security situation in some regions, Somalis' lives remain deeply marked by the combined effects of political instability, recurring humanitarian crises and economic hardship.

Between persistent insecurity and community spirit

In many rural areas, the presence of Al-Shabaab continues to restrict movement, economic activity and access to essential services. Sporadic attacks in major cities such as Mogadishu are a reminder of the fragility of peace, even as Somali forces and their international partners make significant gains. For the population, this means constant vigilance, adapting daily routines and relying heavily on family and community networks for protection and solidarity.

An informal economy that carries the country

With a shortage of formal jobs, the informal economy is the main source of income. Small shops, informal transport, and the sale of food or handicrafts animate urban markets. Remittances from the diaspora remain a central pillar of survival for many families, paying for schooling, healthcare and food. In rural areas, livestock farming, notably of camels, goats and sheep, remains an essential traditional activity, even though repeated droughts are undermining livelihoods.

Climate crises and food insecurity

Climate change has a profound impact on daily life in Somalia. Cycles of drought and flooding follow one another, displacing thousands of people every year. Camps for internally displaced people, often makeshift, shelter entire families who depend on humanitarian aid for water, food and sanitation. Food insecurity, amplified by poor agricultural performance, remains a major concern, despite the increased involvement of NGOs and UN agencies.

Limited access to social services

Access to education and healthcare remains uneven. In cities, private schools and health centres offer relatively acceptable services, but they are out of reach for a large part of the population because of high costs. In rural areas, infrastructure is scarce or non-existent. Women, in particular, face heightened challenges: limited access to maternal care, economic insecurity and the responsibility of running the household in a context of instability.

A young society looking to the future

Despite these difficulties, a new energy is emerging from Somalia's youth, who make up more than 70% of the population. Tech entrepreneurs, artists, athletes and community actors are taking part in a cultural and economic renaissance. In Mogadishu, Hargeisa and Baidoa, modern cafés, start-ups and social initiatives are emerging, driven by a deep desire for stability and development. In Somalia, daily life remains hard, but it is also marked by an exceptional capacity among its people to rebuild, adapt and hope.

Writer: BAWA ALLAH Khadidjatou A.
en.4565:
Moroni, 24 November 2025 (PRESS AFRICA) In the Comoros, a tropical archipelago with strong cultural identities, young people occupy a central demographic place. Bearers of hope in a country where more than 60% of the population is under 25, they nonetheless find themselves at a crossroads, caught up in deep socioeconomic challenges and in the emergence of new behaviors that part of Comorian society describes as "vices."

Mass unemployment and idleness, a fertile breeding ground

The first factor fueling these excesses is economic. Youth unemployment stands at alarming levels, often above 40%, according to various local estimates. Without career prospects, many drift toward activities that may lead them away from traditional values: petty trafficking, use of illicit substances, minor delinquency and gambling dependence.

This precarity creates a sense of frustration that translates into a frantic search for quick ways to "succeed" or simply to survive, sometimes at the expense of social or moral rules.

Risky behaviors

The omnipresence of social media (TikTok, Facebook, Instagram) plays a central role. For many young Comorians, exposure to Westernized or Middle Eastern models is driving a rapid transformation of social codes. There is a rise in cyberbullying, dangerous challenges, early sexualization and the pursuit of online fame through provocative content.

Some young people see it as a space for expression; others turn it into a field of experimentation with sometimes worrying limits, amplified by the absence of local digital regulation.

Consumption of local and imported drugs

Drug use, long taboo, is gaining ground. Kanja (cannabis) remains widespread, but new substances from abroad are circulating in some urban circles. Alcohol, though prohibited under religious norms, is consumed covertly at private parties.

These practices are spreading discreetly but steadily, worrying parents, educators and religious leaders, who see a risk of the collapse of cultural and spiritual reference points.

Petty crime and informal gangs

With few support structures, informal groups of young people are forming in neighborhoods of Moroni, Mutsamudu and Fomboni. While not comparable to the structured gangs of some neighboring countries, these bands nonetheless engage in opportunistic theft, vandalism, nighttime altercations and sporadic assaults. These phenomena remain limited but are enough to fuel a climate of mistrust between generations.

Early marriages, hidden relationships...

Social change also affects the intimate sphere. The gap between a youth seeking autonomy and a society still strongly shaped by religious and family traditions causes ruptures: a rise in clandestine relationships, the circumvention of customary norms, and forced or quickly dissolved marriages. This tension between modernity and tradition fuels a deep malaise among many adolescents.

A weakened education system

The Comorian education system is struggling to absorb population growth. Overcrowded classrooms, recurrent strikes and a lack of career guidance leave many young people to fend for themselves. In this void, deviant behavior finds particularly fertile ground.

The "vices" of young people in the Comoros are not merely individual excesses: they reveal the broader challenges of a nation in transition, torn between tradition and modernity, between economic expectations and structural constraints. The debate remains open, but one thing is certain: the future of the Comoros will depend largely on the collective ability to offer its youth a clear, dignified and stable horizon.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4556:
Antananarivo, 24 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA—For more than two decades, Madagascar has gone through recurring cycles of political instability: disputed elections, abrupt changes of leadership, institutional crises and social tensions. Far from being purely political, these upheavals have left a deep mark on the Malagasy economy, holding back its development and heightening the social vulnerability of a country that nonetheless has immense natural resources.

An unpredictable political climate

One of the first effects of political instability is a loss of confidence among investors, both local and international. With each crisis — 2002, 2009, 2018, 2023 — flows of FDI (foreign direct investment) fall sharply. Companies, particularly in the mining, tourism and textile sectors, adopt a wait-and-see approach. Expansion projects are postponed, some contracts suspended, and several investors prefer to turn to environments seen as more stable, such as Mauritius, Rwanda or Kenya.

For a country where FDI accounts for an essential share of the financing of infrastructure and industry, these setbacks have a direct impact on growth.

Tourism at the mercy of crises

Madagascar has one of the richest biodiversities in the world, making tourism a natural engine of development. But it is also a sector that is extremely sensitive to political crises. With each episode of tension, bookings fall, airlines reduce flight frequencies, and hotel operators record historically low occupancy rates. The lack of stability also harms the international visibility of the destination, which struggles to compete with the giants of the African sector.

Sociopolitical tensions are frequently marked by road closures, port disruptions, strikes and administrative blockages. These dysfunctions directly affect trade, notably exports of vanilla, cloves, lychees and minerals.

The private sector regularly complains of delays, shortages and higher transport costs, which reduce the competitiveness of the Malagasy economy.

A heavy social toll

Political fragility spills over into the population's already precarious living conditions. Government uncertainty often brings runaway inflation, a depreciation of the ariary, higher prices for imported goods, a loss of purchasing power and a rise in poverty, affecting more than 80% of households in some regions.

Businesses, faced with an unstable environment, hesitate to hire or cut their workforces. Young people, who make up the majority of the population, find themselves durably shut out of the labour market.

Suspension of international funding

Donors (the World Bank, the IMF, the European Union) often make their aid conditional on institutional stability. Each crisis leads to a temporary suspension of funding, paralysing infrastructure projects, health and education programmes, administrative reforms and investment in energy and agriculture.

This dependence on international aid makes the Malagasy economy particularly vulnerable to domestic political swings.

An immense but under-exploited economic potential

Despite these obstacles, Madagascar has considerable assets: substantial mineral reserves, vast farmland, unique flora and fauna, and a dynamic youth. However, political instability prevents these riches from being fully harnessed. It creates a vicious circle in which economic stagnation fuels social frustration, which in turn feeds new political tensions.

Analysts believe the key to sustained growth lies in consolidating institutions, transparent electoral reforms, more stable governance and an inclusive national dialogue. Without political stability, they say, economic prospects will remain limited despite the country's exceptional potential.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4557:
Victoria, 24 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA— Known for their idyllic beaches and a political stability that is rare in the region, the Seychelles also cultivate a discreet reputation: that of a financial refuge where, for more than three decades, shell companies, offshore capital and sometimes carefully concealed fortunes have been intertwined. Although the country has undertaken several transparency reforms, its past and certain current practices continue to fuel suspicion that opaque financial flows persist.

A legal architecture tailored for offshore business

From the 1990s, the Seychelles put in place one of the most attractive offshore legislative frameworks in the world. The archipelago offered the rapid creation of international business companies (IBCs), virtually zero taxation for non-resident entities, strict banking secrecy and shareholder registers that were not open to the public.

This framework, designed to attract foreign capital to support an economy with limited resources, was a considerable success… but also led to abuses. Between 2000 and 2018, the number of registered offshore companies sometimes exceeded 10,000 a year, a disproportionate volume for a country of fewer than 100,000 inhabitants.

Capital from everywhere… and from nowhere

With simplified procedures and low costs, the archipelago became a favoured destination for companies seeking to optimise their taxes, for private fortunes wishing to protect their assets, for financial intermediaries operating in the shadows and for players involved in complex cross-border arrangements.

While most of the structures are not illegal, some have been used to conceal beneficial owners, circumvent sanctions, hide assets derived from corruption and facilitate large-scale tax evasion.

The role of company formation firms

A constellation of specialist firms, based in Victoria or operating from Dubai, Hong Kong and even London, has thrived in this market. These intermediaries offered "turnkey" services, including the creation of companies in 24 hours; the provision of nominee directors; associated offshore bank accounts; and financial transfers concealed across several jurisdictions. This industry, long subject to little oversight, helped to sustain an ecosystem conducive to opaque financial arrangements.

A tax haven reputation that is hard to shake off

Despite notable progress, the Seychelles is still regularly singled out by the IMF, the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the European Union and the OECD. In 2020, the archipelago was placed on the European blacklist of tax havens before being removed under conditions. But for many analysts, it remains a grey zone of global finance.

Recent reforms

Under diplomatic pressure, the Seychelles has begun reforms that boil down to strengthening transparency on beneficial owners, tighter control of shell companies, more active cooperation with international investigations, tougher banking rules and improved efforts against money laundering. The government says it wants to clean up the country's image and protect its tourism sector from the fallout of a financial scandal.

Fortunes still in the shadows?

Despite these efforts, experts agree that a significant share of the concealed fortunes is not physically located in the Seychelles, but in legal structures domiciled in the archipelago. In other words, the money circulates through global financial networks but benefits from Seychelles anonymity. Restricted access to registers, even reformed ones, and practices inherited from the past allow some capital to continue hiding there, sometimes with ramifications across several continents.

A fragile balance between attractiveness and transparency

The archipelago must now arbitrate between two contradictory imperatives: preserving its offshore sector, which generates significant revenue, and complying with international standards and avoiding sanctions. This delicate equation will determine the Seychelles' future place in global finance.

Today, the Seychelles is trying to reposition itself as less of a paradise for opaque fortunes, but still attractive enough for discreet capital. The country remains at the heart of a global debate: can economic sovereignty, the need for revenue and the imperative of transparency be reconciled?

Reporter: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4555:
Port Louis, 24 November 2025 – PRESS AFRICA – Often cited as one of the best-performing health systems in the Indian Ocean, Mauritius continues to face a major issue: maternal and child mortality. Despite regular investment, modern infrastructure and near-universal health coverage, the island nation is still struggling with preventable deaths during pregnancy, childbirth and in the first weeks of a newborn's life.

A country ahead of the curve, but not out of danger

Mauritius has a health system that is free of charge to the entire population, a rare asset in the region. Progress made in recent decades, including the expansion of regional hospitals, the strengthening of community-based medicine and vaccination programmes, has significantly reduced maternal and infant mortality rates.

However, some indicators have stagnated for several years, showing that improvement is no longer as rapid. Health authorities acknowledge that the country is reaching a "zone of resistance", where the challenges become more complex and multifactorial.

Obstetric complications: the leading cause of maternal death

The causes linked to maternity remain relatively similar to those seen in other middle-income countries: postpartum haemorrhage, hypertension and pre-eclampsia, infections related to childbirth, and pre-existing conditions aggravated by pregnancy.

While Mauritian hospitals have well-equipped obstetric units, specialists sometimes point to delays in care, particularly in rural areas or among women with comorbidities. The rise of diabetes and hypertension in the general population also complicates the monitoring of pregnancies.

Infant mortality: the toll of premature births

For newborns, the first 48 hours are the most critical.
The factors cited include prematurity, low birth weight, respiratory distress, neonatal infections and congenital malformations.

Mauritius has relatively high-performing neonatal services, but health professionals stress that the quality of antenatal care on the mother's side strongly determines newborn survival, particularly in low-income families.

Social and cultural disparities

Even though access to care is free, some inequalities persist. These include differences between urban areas and more isolated villages, delays in antenatal consultations, a lack of health education, taboos around pregnancy in some communities, and difficulties with transport or family availability. Teenage mothers also remain more vulnerable, exposed to obstetric risks and irregular follow-up.

The growing role of non-communicable diseases

Mauritius is among the countries with the highest rates of diabetes and obesity in the Indian Ocean. These non-communicable diseases (NCDs) have a direct impact on maternal health and foetal growth. The increase in high-risk pregnancies among overweight or diabetic women partly explains the stagnation of progress in reducing maternal and child deaths.

Sustained efforts, but more is needed

The Mauritian government is stepping up initiatives such as early antenatal monitoring campaigns, improvements to neonatal intensive care units, ongoing training of health personnel, the promotion of family planning, and awareness programmes in schools and communities. In addition, partnerships with international organisations support the development of new epidemiological surveillance strategies.

However, experts insist on the need to go further:
strengthening NCD prevention among women of childbearing age, modernising some hospital equipment and improving coordination between primary health centres and hospitals.

A challenge for Mauritius's health future

Reducing maternal and child mortality remains an essential indicator of the country's social development. While Mauritius has climbed to the ranks of Africa's most advanced nations in public health, it must now take on a new stage: guaranteeing every woman and every newborn an optimal level of care, with no gaps or delays.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4538:
Cairo, 24 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA— Long established in Egypt, where it enjoyed a golden age in the 19th and early 20th centuries, freemasonry remains a subject shrouded in opacity today. Banned since the 1960s, closely monitored by the authorities and largely viewed through the lens of religious and political debates, it no longer has a legal or official framework through which the number of its practitioners can be measured precisely. Yet traces of discreet interest and persistent micro-circles continue to raise questions and prompt analysis.

A deep historical presence

Egypt was one of the first countries in Africa and the Middle East to welcome modern freemasonry. As early as 1798, at the time of the Napoleonic campaign, lodges were formed. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, growth was notable: English, French, Scottish and Italian lodges operated there; notables, civil servants and intellectuals joined the lodges, and freemasonry contributed to the cultural and associational life of Cairo and Alexandria.

But from the 1950s and 1960s, successive regimes associated the lodges with potential political risks. In 1964, Masonic activities were suspended by state decision. Since then, no official Masonic structure has operated legally in the country.

A practice that cannot be quantified

In the absence of recognized lodges, Egypt has no official statistics on the number of active freemasons or sympathizers.
Specialist analysts agree on one point: any precise estimate is impossible, because no regular lodge is authorized; declared Masonic activities are prohibited; international Masonic networks no longer list an Egyptian jurisdiction; and the subject remains contentious in the public sphere. The exchanges that do exist therefore point more to informal micro-circles with no institutional recognition.

Informal networks: a discreet but persistent reality

Despite the official bans, several researchers in the sociology of religion and initiatory movements note the existence of private discussion groups, personal ties with foreign obediences, occasional meetings abroad for Egyptians initiated outside the country, and a form of "cultural freemasonry" centered on philosophical, symbolic or historical interest.

These practices remain, however, marginal, scattered and often unstructured. They allow neither a numerical estimate nor a reliable statistical analysis.

A strict legislative environment

Egypt's legal apparatus tightly regulates unauthorized associations. The authorities prohibit the registration of lodges, monitor gatherings perceived as private or clandestine, and restrict any form of undeclared transnational organization.

This environment makes it impossible for a regular, recognized and structured freemasonry to re-emerge, as can be seen in the Maghreb, West Africa or Europe.

Social perceptions: between mistrust, myth and ignorance

In public opinion, freemasonry in Egypt remains poorly understood, often associated with conspiracy theories, linked to secrecy rather than to its real historical legacy, and approached with caution in the media sphere. This context helps keep the subject in shadow rather than light.

A historical influence

Though no longer active as a recognized institution, Egyptian freemasonry survives mainly in cultural memory: former lodge buildings in Alexandria, the archives of European obediences and traces in the biographies of 20th-century political and intellectual figures. However, its real impact is weak today, and its activity is confined to discreet networks mainly oriented toward the outside of the country.

Egypt was one of the great Masonic crossroads of the Middle East.
But in the absence of legal recognition and in a restrictive political environment, the number of current practitioners remains impossible to quantify, and any networks that may exist in no way reflect the historical importance freemasonry once held in the country.

The archipelago of intellectual influences it once represented is now no more than a set of marginal, discreet initiatives disconnected from any official structure.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4540:
24 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA—A sociopolitical legacy claimed by some and loathed by others, it still structures alliances, feeds divisions and shapes ambitions. Thirteen years after the fall of Muammar Gaddafi, Libya continues to live under the heavy shadow of its former leader, as the country still tries to equip itself with unified and stable institutions.

For more than four decades, Muammar Gaddafi built an ultra-centralised regime based on his "Green Book" and a power architecture blending revolutionary committees, tribal networks and control of oil rents.

The fall of the regime was not enough to erase these structures. On the contrary, many local officials who came out of the revolutionary committees have kept a strong community base. Some tribes historically allied with the regime continue to voice support for a return to the order of "before 2011". The fragmented security apparatus has given way to militias that sometimes reproduce practices inherited from the Gaddafi era: centralisation of force, personalisation of local chiefs, a war economy.

Saif al-Islam: the symbol of an expected continuity

While the Gaddafi legacy long remained diffuse, it took concrete form again in 2021 with the reappearance of Saif al-Islam Gaddafi, the presumed heir of the former leader. Although wanted by the International Criminal Court and still shrouded in mystery, Saif al-Islam has managed to mobilise certain tribes in southern and western Libya, to crystallise a nostalgic narrative around a "stable and unified" pre-revolution Libya, and to reinsert himself into the national political debate as an alternative to the current elites, seen as ineffective.

For part of the population, Saif al-Islam represents a potential return to a strong state, able to secure the borders and restart oil production. For others, he embodies the danger of a return to authoritarianism and impunity.

A tribal-political legacy that is still active

Libyan society remains strongly structured by tribes. Gaddafi's regime not only instrumentalised these structures but also organised a subtle balance between them. Since the regime's fall, the tribes formerly allied with power — such as the Kadhadfa or the Warfalla — have been trying to regain their influence. Tribes that were marginalised under Gaddafi, by contrast, are demanding political revenge.

This competition between tribal blocs continues to slow the building of unified institutions, to fuel regional rivalries between Tripoli, Benghazi and Sebha, and to reinforce dependence on local militias.

A political imagination that endures

More than a name, the Gaddafi dynasty has left an imaginary: that of a sovereign state firmly controlling oil rents, of territorial unity imposed by force, and of a pan-Africanist nationalism sometimes tinged with anti-Westernism.

This imaginary now serves as a reference for various political currents, including some military factions aspiring to a return to centralised power.

A divided youth

Young Libyans, who knew the "Guide" only in their childhood or not at all, now face two contradictory narratives: that of a stable but repressive past and that of a free but chaotic present.

This ambivalence translates into a rise in nostalgic discourse in the most marginalised areas and categorical resistance in the regions that paid the heaviest price during the 2011 repression.

A regional influence that can still be felt

The Gaddafi legacy extends beyond Libya's borders. Several African states that benefited from the regime's financial support still watch the evolution of Gaddafist forces on the political scene with interest. The legacy shows in the pan-Africanist networks that remain active, in the trans-Saharan informal economy and in the residual influence of certain former regime officials in neighbouring countries.

A legacy that cannot be bypassed

Post-2011 Libya has never truly managed to shake off its past. Whether one supports or opposes the Gaddafi dynasty, its influence remains a structuring element of the sociopolitical landscape. Attempts at democratic transition, regularly obstructed by power struggles, show that Libya will only be able to move fully forward by undertaking genuine work on memory and institutional refoundation.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4539:
24 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA— Since the early 2000s, Morocco has established itself on the African and Arab stage as a singular case: a kingdom engaged in gradual institutional reform, sustained economic development and an assertive diplomacy. This governance model, often presented as a "Moroccan way" reconciling political stability and modernisation, continues to shape the country's trajectory profoundly. But it also prompts debate about its limits, particularly in local governance, public freedoms and the reduction of social inequalities.

An executive monarchy at the centre of the system

At the heart of the Moroccan governance model lies a constitutional monarchy whose prerogatives remain extensive. King Mohammed VI, in office since 1999, is at once head of state; supreme religious authority (Commander of the Faithful); a major economic player through the royal holdings; and guiding force behind the country's major national strategies.

This centrality ensures a political stability that is rare in the Maghreb region, where several neighbours have experienced chaotic transitions. Royal power acts as an arbiter between institutions, government coalitions and socio-economic actors, which limits institutional crises but reduces the real autonomy of the government.

Institutional reforms under control

The 2011 Constitution, adopted in the context of the Arab Spring, strengthened Parliament and the government, while introducing advances such as the separation of powers, fundamental freedoms and advanced regionalisation, whose implementation remains partial on the ground.

The main strategic levers – diplomacy, security, major economic projects – remain steered by the Palace. This "dual governance" allows strong strategic coherence, but it leads to overlapping responsibilities and weak accountability among political actors.

A recognised but unequal development model

Morocco has succeeded in positioning itself as a regional economic hub, notably through a proactive industrial policy (automotive, aerospace, textiles, phosphates); the development of strategic infrastructure (Tanger Med, roads, ports, high-speed rail); and a firmly embraced economic openness (AfCFTA, EU and US partnerships, African investments).

These choices have produced tangible results, namely growth above the regional average, appeal to foreign investors and technological upgrading in certain sectors.

However, the benefits remain unevenly distributed. This refers to persistent divides between urban and rural areas, high youth unemployment, significant regional disparities despite regionalisation, and an informal economy estimated at between 25 and 30% of GDP.

The New Development Model (NMD) launched in 2021 acknowledges these limits and sets new social objectives, but its implementation remains gradual.

An assumed African leadership

On the continental stage, Rabat pursues a proactive economic diplomacy. This includes, among other things, massive investments in banking, telecoms, insurance and agri-food; religious and cultural cooperation with West Africa; the development of energy and agricultural alliances; and the strategic returns of the Moroccan diaspora in Africa. This positioning has strengthened Morocco's influence, notably in the Sahel and sub-Saharan Africa.

The Sahara question: a structuring pillar

Modern Moroccan governance is built heavily around the Western Sahara question, a major political issue. Recent diplomatic advances — notably US recognition under the Trump administration and the support of several African and Arab countries — reinforce the kingdom's leadership.

However, this issue absorbs a large share of foreign policy, high military budgets and constant diplomatic communication. It remains a point of regional tension and largely conditions internal reforms.

Social progress, but…

Morocco has recorded progress in the fight against poverty, access to healthcare and health insurance (AMO), the extension of social coverage, and women's rights (Moudawana, economic participation).

However, challenges remain, including the slow pace of judicial reform, the limited perceived independence of the media, pressure on human rights defenders and the uneven quality of public education.

A model between stability, control and modernisation

The Moroccan governance model is characterised by a subtle balance based on a strong monarchy that ensures stability and drives the strategic vision; pluralistic political institutions that are still limited in their autonomy; a dynamic but socially unequal economy; and an effective diplomacy backed by growing influence on the continent.

This model has allowed Morocco to maintain an upward trajectory in a regional environment that is often unstable. However, the durability of this governance will depend on its capacity to reduce inequalities, strengthen trust in institutions, speed up regionalisation and modernise political practices. The kingdom is resolutely advancing along a path where stability and reform must now move forward together.

Reporter: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4537:
Tunis, 24 November 2025 – PRESS AFRICA –Long oriented towards the Mediterranean and Europe, Tunisia is gradually reshaping its geopolitical outlook to anchor itself more firmly in Africa's dynamics. While its historical position naturally ties it to the Maghreb, internal crises and the continent's geopolitical shifts are pushing Tunis to broaden its diplomatic and economic horizons beyond its traditional partners.

But what is Tunisia's real share in African integration? What levers is it using, and what obstacles still hold back its engagement?

An underused geographical position

Located at the junction of North Africa, the Sahel and the Mediterranean, Tunisia has major assets for becoming a bridge between Europe and Africa. Yet for decades, this African dimension was relegated to the background in favour of a strengthened partnership with the European Union, an economic anchoring centred on the Mediterranean and a diplomacy turned towards the Arab world.

The post-2011 political transition prompted the country to reconsider its continental role, notably because of its sought-after diversification of economic partners, growing competition with other Maghreb countries and the opening of new African markets, particularly in ICT, health and higher education.

A reactivated African diplomacy

In recent years, Tunis has strengthened its presence on the African stage by relying on a growing number of economic missions in West and Central Africa; technical cooperation partnerships in the fields of training, health and public administration; and a reaffirmation of its policy of openness to the African market through the AfCFTA, which Tunisia ratified in 2020.

The country is also working to consolidate its role within the African Union, the African Development Bank (AfDB), based in Abidjan, and COMESA, which it joined in 2018. These memberships reflect Tunisia's desire to integrate more deeply into African value chains.

Tunisian sectors already established in Africa

Despite limited means, certain Tunisian sectors have succeeded in making their mark in several African countries. They include, in particular, health, education, information technology and construction and public works.

Health: Tunisian medical missions are deployed in more than ten African countries. Tunisian clinics welcome thousands of African patients each year for specialist care.

Higher education: Tunisian private universities are attracting a growing share of French-speaking African students. Educational cooperation agreements are multiplying with Central and West Africa.

Information technology: Tunisian ICT companies offer solutions in e-government, banking digitalisation and cybersecurity. They take part in administrative modernisation projects in several African capitals.

Public works and engineering: Tunisian design offices are present in the construction of road, energy and health infrastructure.

What about internal turbulence and diplomacy?

Tunisia's potential, however, remains hampered by major challenges, including political instability since 2011, a persistent economic slowdown, high public debt, recurring social tensions and an administration that is at times cumbersome and slow to react.

These constraints limit Tunisia's capacity to carry major continental projects or to rival other African powers such as Morocco, Algeria, Egypt or South Africa.

Between a weakened Maghreb and a changing Africa

One of the obstacles to Tunisia's African integration remains the absence of Maghreb momentum. The deadlock of the Arab Maghreb Union (AMU) reduces, in particular, Tunisia's regional economic reach, the possibility of forming a coherent North African bloc and the country's diplomatic weight in continental negotiations. The Algerian-Moroccan standoff and the closure of the border between Rabat and Algiers complicate any shared vision of North Africa.

The AfCFTA: an opportunity to seize

Tunisia sees in the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) a way to diversify its exports, attract investment, become a Mediterranean-African hub and develop its SMEs towards sub-Saharan markets.

A remarkable intellectual and cultural contribution

Beyond the economy, Tunisia plays an important role in African academic output, in forums on democracy and governance, and in the circulation of ideas and of French-speaking African elites. Tunisian culture, renowned for its openness and cosmopolitanism, continues to project the country across the continent.

A real share, but one still in the making

Tunisia's participation in African integration is modest but real, promising but still limited. But to become a major player in African integration, Tunis will have to stabilise its political scene, modernise its administration, strengthen its logistics infrastructure and clarify its long-term African strategy.

Tunisia has the skills, the knowledge and the geographical position to play a more ambitious role. It remains to give it the political, economic and institutional means to match its ambitions.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4528:
Algiers, 24 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA— Algeria, a crossroads country between the Sahel, the Maghreb and the Mediterranean, has for more than a decade welcomed a growing number of sub-Saharan nationals. They come from Mali, Niger, Chad, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea and several other countries in West and Central Africa. Some are merely in transit to Europe, but others settle temporarily or long-term in Algeria's major cities.

While the country remains one of the region's most attractive economic hubs, the lives of Black Africans in Algeria are still marked by numerous socioeconomic and security challenges, often exacerbated by migration tensions and social perceptions.

A mixed welcome: individual hospitality, collective social pressure

In daily life, many Black Africans report receiving gestures of solidarity, particularly in working-class neighborhoods, markets and mosques.
But at the same time, the collective perception remains ambivalent, fueled in particular by the visible increase in migration flows, social anxiety aggravated by the economic crisis, a lack of public policy to regulate migration, and cultural and linguistic tensions.

This duality (individual hospitality, institutional rigidity) creates a fragile coexistence, in which sub-Saharan migrants and residents adapt as best they can.

Economic precarity: the reality of odd jobs

For the majority, professional integration remains very difficult. Without a clear legal status, opportunities are often limited to informal work such as cleaning, handling, security guarding and other construction-related jobs. These poorly paid jobs expose workers, among other things, to exploitation by certain intermediaries, wages that are sometimes unpaid, long and arduous days, and a total lack of social protection. According to several local NGOs, this vulnerability is aggravated by the impossibility of obtaining official contracts, which creates strong economic dependence.

Housing, between squalor and instability

Access to decent housing is one of the biggest obstacles.
Many live in shared rooms, in buildings under construction, in outlying neighborhoods or in informal rentals that are particularly expensive. This precarity is heightened by a lack of recognized identity documents, the mistrust or reluctance of some landlords and, above all, the fear of evictions, which are sometimes sudden.

Difficult access to healthcare

Living conditions, often cramped and insecure, weaken families and isolated workers. Although hospital emergency rooms can take in anyone in distress, the reality is more complex for Black Africans, who face limited access to the health system, sometimes prohibitive care costs, a lack of insurance and isolated discrimination in some facilities. For many migrants, self-medication or recourse to community networks remains common.

Racism and discrimination: a reality still present

The subject is sensitive, but impossible to ignore. Several Black Africans report insults in the street, job refusals linked to skin color, frequent police checks and isolated assaults, sometimes serious. Even though part of society firmly condemns such behavior, racial discrimination does exist, fueled by migration tensions, mutual cultural ignorance, certain representations inherited from the past and polarizing media discourse. Algerian and international associations are working to raise public awareness, but the road remains long.

The question of expulsions and police checks

One of the most controversial issues concerns operations to round up sub-Saharan migrants and return them to the country's southern borders, notably those with Niger. These operations, denounced by some NGOs, are sparking a national debate. For the state, the aim is to control irregular migration flows and guarantee security. For associations, these practices lack transparency and endanger vulnerable people.

A resilient community, organized around mutual aid networks

Faced with hardship, Black Africans settled in Algeria rely on powerful community networks, religious groups (churches, African mosques), digital platforms and informal associations that facilitate employment, housing and moral support. This resilience partly explains why some are able to put down lasting roots in the social fabric.

The situation of Black Africans in Algeria reflects a continental phenomenon: the transformation of migration routes, the recomposition of African identities and the tensions generated by the globalization of movement.

While gestures of solidarity and citizen initiatives exist, difficulties remain numerous. Algeria, a hinge country between Black Africa and the Maghreb, has the opportunity to become a model of welcome and coexistence. But this transformation will require sustained institutional, social and cultural efforts.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4527:
24 November 2025 —PRESS AFRICA— Djibouti, a small strategic nation in the Horn of Africa, has established itself as a major logistics and trade hub thanks to its ports and its proximity to international shipping routes. However, despite its assets, the country presents specific risks that deserve particular attention for any economic initiative.

Geopolitical and security risks

Djibouti's stability is influenced by the volatile situation in the region, notably in Somalia and Ethiopia. Companies must avoid underestimating the potential impact of regional tensions on maritime transport, cross-border trade and the safety of expatriates. Recommendation: it is important to regularly assess geopolitical alerts and establish security protocols for teams and critical infrastructure.

Economic concentration and sectoral dependence

The Djiboutian economy depends heavily on port activities and on logistics linked to foreign military bases. This dependence makes the country vulnerable to external shocks and to fluctuations in international markets. To address this, investments need to be diversified across different sectors (renewable energy, ICT, resilient agriculture) to reduce vulnerability and increase economic resilience.

Social and environmental challenges

Unemployment, social inequality and internal migration remain major issues. In addition, drought and water stress are persistent environmental risks that can affect local production and social stability. On this front, sustainable practices and corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiatives should be built in to strengthen local acceptance and minimise environmental impacts.

Regulation and transparency

Despite business-friendly reforms, bureaucracy and some risks of corruption remain, especially in sectors with heavy interaction with public authorities. To this end, it is urgent to comply scrupulously with local standards, adopt internal audits and work with reliable local partners to secure operations.

Logistics and infrastructure

Although Djibouti has high-performing ports, inland infrastructure remains limited for some industrial and agricultural zones. Companies must anticipate transport and storage constraints. Ideally, tailored logistics strategies should be put in place in partnership with local operators, along with investment in efficient storage and transport solutions.

Djibouti offers considerable potential for international investors and businesses, thanks to its strategic position and port assets. However, a cautious and structured approach is essential. Understanding the geopolitical, social and environmental risks, diversifying investment sectors and adopting practices that comply with local regulations are key factors in securing and sustaining projects in this fast-expanding market.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4529:
Asmara, 24 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA— Eritrea, a Horn of Africa country long isolated on the international stage, is now revealing a remarkable cultural potential that could appeal to international markets. Through traditional music, refined crafts and a distinctive cuisine, the Eritrean nation is establishing itself as a land where authenticity meets exportability.

Music and performing arts, a heritage to share

Eritrean music, shaped by African and Arab influences, offers unique sounds thanks to traditional instruments such as the krar, the washint and the kebero. These instruments, which accompany folk songs and dances, bear witness to an intangible heritage that already appeals to international festivals. Eritrean dance companies and musical groups are beginning to perform abroad, introducing international audiences to rhythms and performances that are still little known.

Crafts and textiles, treasures of authenticity
Eritrean crafts are another export lever. Traditional weaving, pottery and silver jewellery engraved with ancestral motifs find a potential market among enthusiasts of ethnic and sustainable products. The tibeb, a distinctive embroidery pattern, could become a signature of the Eritrean textile industry internationally, in the same way as certain African craft trends that are already being exported successfully.

Cuisine: new flavours for the world
Eritrean cuisine, notably its dishes based on injera (a fermented flatbread made from teff) and spicy sauces, has the potential to attract international markets. Local initiatives are beginning to develop restaurant concepts and ready-to-export food products, allowing foreign consumers to taste a cuisine that is still little represented beyond the country's borders.

Challenges and opportunities

Despite these assets, the promotion of Eritrean culture internationally remains held back by insufficient tourism and cultural infrastructure, as well as by logistical difficulties. However, the local authorities, aware of the cultural and economic value of these resources, are stepping up efforts to create cultural exchange programmes, take part in international trade fairs and facilitate the export of crafts.

Eritrean culture, still largely unknown, has considerable potential to become an international showcase of the country's identity. Through music, crafts and cuisine, Eritrea has every asset it needs to turn its cultural heritage into a sustainable and profitable export, thereby contributing to its visibility on the world stage and to the diversification of its economy.

Reporter: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4517:
Johannesburg, 19 November 2025 – PRESS AFRICA – South Africa remains one of the most developed countries on the African continent, but its Human Development Index (HDI) reveals a more contrasting reality than it appears. Between economic progress, persistent inequality and social challenges, the Rainbow Nation is still trying to reconcile growth and fairness.

An HDI edging up, but still unequal

According to the latest report of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), South Africa posts an HDI of 0.713 in 2025, placing the country in the "high human development" category. This figure keeps it at the top of the sub-Saharan Africa rankings, alongside Mauritius (0.805) and Seychelles (0.798).

This performance rests on modern infrastructure, a diversified economy (mining, the automotive industry, finance, tourism) and relatively broad access to education and healthcare. However, behind this facade of progress, the gaps between social classes and regions remain wide.

Social divides hold back progress

Despite public policies focused on reducing inequality, nearly 18 million South Africans still live below the poverty line, according to World Bank estimates. Unemployment, which affects around 31% of the active population, remains one of the highest on the continent.

Rural areas, particularly in Limpopo and KwaZulu-Natal provinces, suffer from a structural lag in education, access to drinking water and sanitation infrastructure. Conversely, large cities such as Johannesburg and Cape Town concentrate wealth and opportunity.

Health and education: the pillars of fragile development

On health, South Africa has made notable progress in the fight against HIV/AIDS. The prevalence rate, once above 20%, is now estimated at 13% thanks to a free, large-scale antiretroviral treatment policy. Average life expectancy, meanwhile, has risen to 65 years, from 52 years in the early 2000s.

In education, the literacy rate now stands at 94%, and higher education is attracting a growing number of African students. However, the poor quality of public schooling and the brain drain abroad continue to limit the benefits of these advances.

Towards more inclusive development

The South African government has launched several initiatives to promote inclusive growth, notably the "Vision 2030" plan, inspired by the National Development Plan. This plan aims to reduce poverty to below 10%, raise life expectancy to 70 years and create millions of sustainable jobs through the energy transition and new technologies.

But the success of this ambition will depend on fighting corruption, strengthening democratic institutions and achieving a better redistribution of wealth.

South Africa remains an unavoidable African power, with considerable economic and human potential. However, its development is still held back by deep inequalities and social divides inherited from apartheid. The improvement in its Human Development Index, though encouraging, will be sustainable only if it establishes equitable growth centred on people, education and social justice.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4518:
Luanda, 19 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA— Nearly half a century after its independence, Angola continues to have an ambiguous relationship with democracy. Between stated willingness to reform and the persistence of authoritarian practices, the southern African country is moving cautiously along the path of democratic governance.

A still fragile political pluralism

Since the end of the civil war in 2002, Angola has equipped itself with modern democratic institutions: a multiparty Constitution, a Parliament elected by universal suffrage, and a National Electoral Commission supposed to guarantee the transparency of the vote. However, the People's Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA), in power since 1975, still dominates the political scene.

The 2022 general elections, narrowly won by President João Lourenço, revealed a more critical society and a galvanized opposition, notably with the UNITA party, led by Adalberto Costa Júnior. Although the vote was described as "broadly peaceful," several observers, including the European Union, noted a lack of fairness in access to the media and irregularities in the vote count.

Reforms and limits of the Lourenço administration

Having come to power in 2017, João Lourenço had promised an era of transparency, anti-corruption efforts and modernization of institutions. Some progress is undeniable: several relatives of former president José Eduardo dos Santos have been targeted by the courts, and Angola has begun a more liberal economic opening.

But politically, criticism persists. Civil society denounces the ruling party's continued grip on institutions and strict control of press freedom. Demonstrations are often repressed, and political activists or overly critical journalists face intimidation or arbitrary arrest.

Freedom of expression: a space under surveillance

Independent media exist in Angola, but their room for maneuver remains limited. Most of the major channels and newspapers are close to those in power or under the state's economic influence. Social media, increasingly used by Angolan youth, have become a new space for debate and protest, much to the dismay of the authorities, who are stepping up digital surveillance.

Human rights organizations, such as Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, have repeatedly warned of growing restrictions on freedom of expression and the repression of peaceful gatherings.

A youth hungry for change

Nearly 65% of Angolans are under 30, a connected, educated generation increasingly demanding of its leaders. These young people are calling for more transparency, jobs and civic participation. Citizen movements, such as "Mudei!" ("I have changed"), are multiplying to encourage political engagement outside the MPLA's traditional system.

However, faced with disillusionment and unemployment, many still choose exile or abstention, a sign of a crisis of confidence in the political system.

An uncertain but hopeful future

Angola today stands at a crossroads. While the country has avoided the most extreme authoritarian excesses of some of its neighbors, it remains far from a consolidated democracy. The next elections, scheduled for 2027, will be a decisive test of the sincerity of the reforms undertaken by President Lourenço.
