International observers stress that the vitality of civil society and the political awakening of youth could, in the long term, profoundly transform Angolan political culture.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4508:
Gaborone, 19 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA— Often cited as an example of stability and good governance in Africa, Botswana also stands out for its ambitious education policies. The country has one of the highest rates of access to education on the continent, but it must now take up a new challenge: improving the quality and fairness of its school system.

Near-universal access to primary school

According to the latest report from Botswana's Ministry of Education and Skills Development, more than 97% of children aged 6 to 12 are in school. This rate, one of the highest in sub-Saharan Africa, is the result of a proactive policy in place since independence in 1966.

The government devotes nearly 20% of its national budget to education, a figure above the African average. Public schools are free up to the end of secondary level, and the state provides textbooks, meals and, in some rural areas, transport.

"Education is the key to development and human dignity," the Minister of Education, Dr Keneilwe Motsumi, said recently when presenting the sector's 2025 figures.

Inequalities between rural and urban areas

Despite this impressive progress, regional disparities remain marked. In remote areas such as Ngamiland and Kgalagadi, a lack of infrastructure and qualified staff holds back full school attendance.

Children from pastoralist and San (Bushmen) communities are particularly vulnerable: nearly 15% of them leave school before the end of the primary cycle, often to help their families with subsistence economic activities.

Local NGOs, such as Education for All Botswana, are calling for stronger inclusion programmes and better cultural adaptation of educational content.

Secondary education on the rise

Access to secondary education has risen sharply: nearly 80% of adolescents aged 13 to 18 are now enrolled in junior or senior secondary school, compared with barely 60% fifteen years ago.

However, the completion rate remains low, at around 65%. The main causes of dropping out are poverty, early pregnancies and the distance between home and school.

In 2024, the government launched the "Re Thuto Tota" ("Let us learn together") programme, which aims to build 200 new rural high schools and equip every pupil with a subsidised laptop by 2027.

The question of quality and graduate unemployment

While Botswana can be proud of having put almost all its children in school, the quality of teaching remains a major concern. National assessments show that nearly 40% of primary pupils struggle with reading and mathematics.

The country also faces a paradox: high unemployment among young graduates, estimated at 26%. "We have succeeded in opening schools, but not yet in linking education to the labour market," admits an official at the Ministry of Labour.

Reforms are under way to modernise curricula, introduce more technical and digital training, and strengthen partnerships between schools and local businesses.

A political will that remains firm

Despite these challenges, Botswana remains a regional model of sustainable education policy. Its steady commitment to universal education has helped raise living standards, reduce poverty and strengthen national cohesion.

For the director of the Education Research Centre in Gaborone, Ms Teboho Rasego, "Botswana proves that investing in education is not a luxury, but a strategy for survival and progress for African countries."

Botswana has won the battle for access to education, but the battle for quality and fairness is still to be fought. To remain an example on the continent, the country will have to train more teachers, narrow the gaps between towns and countryside, and above all adapt its education system to the needs of a changing economy.
en.4504:
Maputo, 19 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA— Mozambique, rich in fertile land and a climate well suited to agricultural production, remains a country where the land feeds both the population and the economy. In 2025, agriculture remains one of the main levers of national development, accounting for about 23% of gross domestic product (GDP) and employing nearly 70% of the working population. Yet despite its potential, the sector is struggling to modernise and to take full advantage of its resources.

A sector vital to economic and social stability

According to data from Mozambique's Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development, the country has 36 million hectares of arable land, of which less than 20% is currently farmed. The main crops are maize, cassava, rice, cotton, sugar cane and cashew nuts, the latter being one of the country's flagship export products.

"Agriculture is the backbone of our economy. It guarantees food security and supports the incomes of millions of Mozambicans," Celso Correia, the Minister of Agriculture, said recently.

In rural areas, notably in the provinces of Nampula, Sofala and Zambezia, family farming dominates, accounting for more than 90% of national food production.

A solid but vulnerable contribution

Although agriculture contributes greatly to Mozambique's GDP growth, it remains heavily dependent on climate hazards. Floods, droughts and cyclones — such as Idai in 2019 and Freddy in 2023 — have underlined the fragility of the Mozambican farming model, which is still little mechanised and insufficiently irrigated.

In 2024, agricultural losses linked to natural disasters were estimated at more than $200 million, affecting thousands of smallholders. This reliance on rainfall explains the low average productivity, estimated at 1.2 tonnes of maize per hectare, compared with more than 4 tonnes in neighbouring South Africa.

Modernisation efforts under way

The government has launched several programmes to strengthen the sector's resilience, notably the National Agricultural Investment Plan (PNIA II 2021-2025), supported by the African Development Bank and the FAO. The plan aims to increase productivity, diversify crops and promote sustainable irrigation.

Foreign investment is also beginning to grow in agribusiness and local value chains, notably in cashew nut processing and sugar production.

Digital farming cooperative projects have emerged in the northern provinces, enabling farmers to access urban markets and obtain credit through mobile platforms.

"We want to move from subsistence farming to commercial agriculture, capable of creating jobs and generating competitive exports," President Filipe Nyusi said in a speech delivered in Beira in October 2025.

Persistent challenges: infrastructure, financing and training

Despite this progress, several obstacles still hold back the sector's transformation. The lack of infrastructure — rural roads, warehouses, irrigation systems — raises costs and limits access to markets.

Agricultural financing also remains a major problem: less than 5% of national bank loans go to farmers, for lack of sufficient collateral. In addition, technical training and agricultural extension services remain inadequate to meet farmers' needs.

Farmers' organisations are demanding a better policy of support for smallholders, notably targeted subsidies and a reduction in taxes on inputs.

Towards sustainable and inclusive agriculture

Faced with climate and socio-economic challenges, Mozambique is seeking to build a more resilient, inclusive and sustainable agriculture. Local initiatives around agroecology and organic farming are multiplying, backed by NGOs and international partners.

The country is also betting on new agricultural technologies, such as drones for land mapping and mobile apps for crop management. These innovations offer a glimmer of hope for a new generation of farmers who are more connected and productive.

Mozambican agriculture remains an essential pillar of the national economy and a key factor of social stability. Its contribution to GDP remains vital, but its potential is still largely under-exploited. For the sector to play its full role as an engine of development, Mozambique will need to step up mechanisation, strengthen land tenure security and diversify its agricultural exports. Between tradition and modernity, the country is at a turning point: that of transforming its agriculture into a genuine lever for sustainable and shared growth.

Reporter: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4503:
Windhoek, 19 November 2025 – PRESS AFRICA – At 72, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah became, on 21 March 2025, the first woman to take Namibia's presidency. Her political career, marked by exile, the struggle for independence and then numerous ministerial responsibilities, makes her both an emblematic and an experienced figure in Namibian governance.

Youth and early commitment

Born on 29 October 1952 in Onamutai, then in "South West Africa", she is the ninth of 13 children. Her father was an Anglican pastor. In her teens she joined SWAPO (South West Africa People's Organisation), the liberation movement, which led her to become actively engaged against South Africa's apartheid regime.

In 1973, in the face of repression, she went into exile. During her years in exile, she studied abroad: a year in the Soviet Union, then in the United Kingdom, where she obtained a master's degree in diplomatic studies. These experiences shaped her profile as a diplomat and career politician.

Political career and responsibilities

Since Namibia's move to independence in 1990, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah has held a range of posts:

  • Member of the National Assembly since 1990.
  • Minister of Women Affairs and Child Welfare (2000-2005); Minister of Information and Broadcasting (2005-2010); Minister of Environment and Tourism (2010-2012); Minister of International Relations (2012-2015, then 2015-2024) and Deputy Prime Minister from 2015.
  • In 2017, she became vice-president of the SWAPO party, the first woman to hold that role.
  • In November 2024, she was elected president with around 57% of the vote, becoming Namibia's fifth president and the first woman to hold the office.

Her rise to the presidency came with a message of continuity and reform. In her inaugural address, she said that "the work that lies ahead is to preserve the gains of our independence … and to ensure shared prosperity".

Priorities for her term and main challenges

At the start of her presidency, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah set several key priorities, notably: diversifying the Namibian economy, which is still heavily dependent on mining and export resources; creating jobs on a massive scale for young people, as youth unemployment remains a major challenge in a country of about 3 million people; reducing inequality, in a context where Namibia is among the most unequal countries in the world; and more efficient management of the state, with the cabinet cut to 14 ministers and 7 deputies, promoting leaner governance.

A symbol of progress for women

The election of Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah marks a major turning point for Namibia and, more broadly, for southern Africa. By becoming the country's first female president, she sends a strong signal about the place of women in political life. She herself has said she wants to be "judged on her competence, and not only because I am a woman".

A critical perspective

Despite her solid CV and political longevity, some challenges remain to be overcome: the SWAPO party, in power since 1990, is seeing its popularity decline; the 2024 elections suffered logistical failures; and her term will have to be judged by concrete results: job creation, reduced inequality and a better distribution of wealth.

Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah embodies both the legacy of Namibia's struggle for independence and the promise of renewed leadership. Her journey, from young activist in exile to head of state, illustrates the political maturing of a country born in 1990. Her term opens a new era: that of a Namibia seeking to combine stability, social justice and economic transformation. But as is often the case, the stakes are high, and only time will tell whether this presidency marks a turning point in the country's history.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4496:
Maseru, 16 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA—In the heart of the southern African mountains, Lesotho is increasingly betting on its youth to revive an economy in search of diversification. With a population of which more than 60% is under 30, the small kingdom enclaved within South Africa has a major demographic asset. But the contribution of this young workforce to the economy remains hampered by unemployment, precarity and a lack of technical training.

A large but underemployed youth

According to data from the Lesotho Bureau of Statistics (BOS), young people make up nearly two-thirds of the working population, but more than 35% of them are unemployed. Many work in informal jobs in agriculture, tailoring or small-scale urban trade.

"The potential of our youth is considerable, but it is still underused. We must turn this energy into a productive force," said Thabo Sofonia, Minister of Labour and Employment, at the Maseru economic forum last October.

The formal sector, dominated by the textile industry, subsistence agriculture and remittances from migrant workers in South Africa, is struggling to absorb the thousands of young graduates entering the labor market each year.

Textiles, the leading employer of young people

For two decades, Lesotho has been one of the main garment exporters in sub-Saharan Africa, notably to the United States thanks to the AGOA trade agreement. The garment factories, concentrated in the capital Maseru and in the industrial zones of Maputsoe, employ nearly 40,000 people, more than 70% of whom are young women.

This sector is a genuine lifeline of jobs for young people, but working conditions are often precarious: low wages, no social protection and dependence on fluctuations in the international market.

"We work hard, but our income does not always allow us to meet our needs," says ’Makhotso, 24, a worker in a garment factory in Maputsoe.

Agriculture, the forgotten pillar of rural youth

In rural areas, where more than half of the population still lives, subsistence farming remains the main economic activity. Young people play an essential role in producing maize, wheat and vegetables.

However, the sector's low profitability, climate change and lack of access to credit hold back their engagement. The government is trying to steer young people toward agribusiness and modern farming cooperatives, through the "Youth Agripreneur Lesotho" program, launched in 2023 with the support of the African Development Bank.

"The future of our country lies in innovative agriculture, run by young people trained in new technologies," says ’Mathato Molapo, the program's coordinator.

Migration and the weight of remittances

Historically, thousands of young Basotho have emigrated to neighboring South Africa, notably to work in the gold and platinum mines. Although this migration has declined since the decline of South Africa's mining sector, migrant remittances still account for nearly 15% of national GDP.

This income plays a vital role in household consumption and children's education, but dependence on it makes the economy vulnerable to external shocks.

Entrepreneurship and training: levers of renewal

Faced with a lack of formal jobs, more and more young people are turning to entrepreneurship. Local start-ups are emerging in digital technology, recycling and crafts, often supported by incubators such as the Bacha Entrepreneurship Project.

The government, for its part, has expanded vocational training programs through the National Training Centre for Technical Skills, in order to equip young people with the skills needed in construction, mechanics and renewable energy.

Despite these efforts, economic analysts believe the transition to a more inclusive economy will take time. "Lesotho must turn its youth into productive human capital. That requires an education policy adapted to the market and a better business climate," stresses Dr. Palesa Mokete, an economist at the National University of Lesotho.

A future to build

Lesotho's young workforce is both its greatest wealth and its greatest challenge. If properly supervised, trained and integrated, it could become the engine of sustainable, diversified growth. But without sufficient investment in education, technology and rural infrastructure, there is a real risk of an entire generation remaining on the margins of economic development.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4495:
Mbabane, 15 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA— In the small kingdom of Eswatini, formerly Swaziland, public health remains one of the most fragile areas of national governance. Despite some progress in medical coverage and in the fight against the major pandemics, the country faces a limited healthcare base, unable to meet the growing demand of a population undergoing demographic change.

An undersized health system

With a little over 1.2 million inhabitants, Eswatini has 30 public hospitals and around 300 primary healthcare centres, according to Ministry of Health figures. In theory these facilities cover the whole territory, but in practice they are often poorly equipped, understaffed and lacking essential medical resources.

The country devotes less than 8% of its national budget to health, a ratio below African Union recommendations. "Our hospitals are overwhelmed, especially in rural areas where a single doctor sometimes serves more than 15,000 people," laments Dr Nhlanhla Dlamini, a practitioner at Hhohho Regional Hospital.

The persistence of the major pandemics

Eswatini remains one of the countries most affected by HIV/AIDS in the world, with a prevalence of around 26% among adults. While the government has succeeded in making antiretrovirals widely available, the health system continues to bear the weight of this pandemic, which absorbs a large share of medical resources.

Prevention campaigns have reduced the number of new infections, but the country must now confront a resurgence of non-communicable diseases — diabetes, hypertension, cancers — for which screening and treatment equipment remains scarce.

"We focused our efforts on HIV for decades, but other silent diseases are now taking over," warns Sibongile Maseko, head nurse at Manzini Hospital.

Ageing infrastructure and a glaring shortage of equipment

In several public facilities, operating theatres and laboratories are more than twenty years old. Stock-outs of essential medicines are frequent, particularly in rural areas.

Power cuts and a lack of drinking water further complicate care. In Nhlangano, for example, patients sometimes travel more than 50 kilometres to find a centre with even a basic X-ray machine.

Medical staff, chronically understaffed, face a gruelling workload. Many choose to emigrate to neighbouring South Africa, which pays better. This brain drain further weakens an already breathless system.

Modernisation efforts still timid

King Mswati III's government launched the "National Health Improvement Plan 2023-2028" in 2023, a programme to modernise infrastructure and strengthen medical staffing. Several regional hospitals are to be renovated, and a pilot digital hospital project has been launched in Mbabane with World Bank support.

However, for lack of sustainable funding, these initiatives are moving slowly. Partnerships with the Global Fund and the World Health Organization (WHO) help ensure the continuity of essential care, but dependence on external aid remains worrying.

"Eswatini must invest more in its own health system. Without financial autonomy, we will not be able to build a solid healthcare base," says Dr Nomusa Simelane, a health economist.

Rural health, the great forgotten area

In mountainous and remote areas, the situation is even more critical. A lack of passable roads, transport and medical centres leads many residents to turn to traditional medicine.

Community midwives still handle nearly 30% of births outside hospital facilities. While their role is essential, obstetric complications remain frequent and maternal mortality remains high: around 300 deaths per 100,000 live births, according to the WHO.

A youth in need of care and hope

Young people, who make up more than 50% of the population, are particularly vulnerable. Unemployment, early pregnancies and sexually transmitted infections weigh heavily on health services.

Local initiatives, such as the "Youth Health Corners" programme, have emerged to offer tailored medical and psychological support, but their coverage remains limited to a few urban districts.

A health system to be rebuilt…

Eswatini faces a structural health challenge: modernising its health system while preserving the gains in the fight against HIV and meeting the new needs of a young and vulnerable population. Without a strong budgetary commitment, better staff training and stronger rural infrastructure, the kingdom's healthcare base risks remaining fragile and unequal. But behind the cracks, hope remains: that of a generation of health workers, NGOs and citizens determined to build, step by step, a health system worthy of the resilience of the Swazi people.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI

Cotonou, 11 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA— The African Guarantee and Economic Cooperation Fund (FAGACE) has passed a major milestone in defining its medium-term vision. On Thursday 30 October 2025, the institution held a consultation workshop at the Fund's headquarters in Cotonou, bringing together its technical and financial partners and marking the official launch of preparatory work on the 2026-2030 Strategic Plan.

Chaired by Director General Dr Ngueto Tiraïna YAMBAYE, the meeting continues the structural reforms under way for several years to modernise FAGACE, strengthen its impact and consolidate its position as a key player in development financing in Africa.

A participatory approach in the service of lasting transformation

In his opening address, Dr Ngueto Tiraïna YAMBAYE recalled that the drawing up of this new strategic plan meets a twofold requirement: to sustain the gains of the reforms under way and to anticipate the continent's economic changes. In this spirit, the planning process adopted rests on a participatory and inclusive approach, guaranteeing the full involvement of the various stakeholders.

Member states, technical and financial partners, and the Fund's staff are thus closely involved in the strategic reflection. The aim is to co-build a document carrying a shared vision, aligned with the real needs of African countries and with the new challenges of sustainable development, the energy transition and the continent's economic sovereignty.

Towards a new strategic direction

The discussions during the workshop laid the foundations for FAGACE's future direction for the period 2026-2030. This direction will be built around major pillars such as strengthening the Fund's financial soundness, diversifying its intervention instruments, promoting the African private sector and supporting public development policies.

Dr YAMBAYE stressed the importance of innovation, rigour and cooperation in implementing this new roadmap. In his view, the next strategic plan must reflect FAGACE's desire to be not only a financing lever, but also a catalyst for partnerships and an engine of economic transformation in the service of Africa.

A collaborative process for a shared vision

The 30 October workshop allowed participants to share their expectations, recommendations and contributions with a view to enriching the collective reflection. These inputs will feed into the technical work leading to the validation of the final document in the coming months.

By initiating this open and collaborative approach, Dr Ngueto Tiraïna YAMBAYE reaffirms his commitment to anchoring FAGACE's governance in consultation, transparency and performance. The 2026-2030 Strategic Plan is thus intended to reflect a shared vision, bringing inclusive growth and lasting prosperity to all of the Fund's member states.

Through this initiative, FAGACE confirms its determination to adapt its action to the changing realities of the continent and to strengthen its central role in promoting productive investment. The process under way opens the way to a new era of performance, impact and economic solidarity, placing the institution at the heart of African development priorities for the coming decade. Thus, under the leadership of Dr Ngueto Tiraïna YAMBAYE, a participatory approach is taking hold to build the Fund's future.

Addis Ababa, 5 November 2025 – PRESS AFRICA – Ethiopia's latest economic review shows a marked improvement in its external debt profile, but also a strong vulnerability that continues to weigh on its development path.

An encouraging decline, but fragility persists

According to a recently published report by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Ethiopia's public and publicly guaranteed debt stood at 34.8% of GDP at the end of June 2024, compared with 40.2% a year earlier and 48.9% at the end of 2021/22. More precisely, external public debt as a share of GDP stood at 15.0% on the same date, down from 18.1% the previous year.

Another key indicator: the "present value of external public debt / GDP" ratio is estimated at 19.1% for 2023, and could climb back to 21.8% in 2025. These figures suggest that Ethiopia is managing to moderate its external financial dependence, that is, its capacity to finance its needs through external debt, in an economic context marked by challenges.

Why this dependence?

Several factors explain this dynamic. The country has historically relied on external borrowing (bilateral, multilateral, Eurobonds) to finance its investment and infrastructure programmes. According to the African Development Bank (AfDB), between 2007 and 2023 Ethiopia's external debt rose from $2.3 billion (10% of GDP) to $27.8 billion (17.1% of GDP), a nearly twelvefold increase.

The country faces strong constraints on domestic resources (tax mobilisation, national savings) and must meet high investment needs. Exposure to currency risk is high: a significant share of the debt is denominated in foreign currencies, which makes Ethiopia sensitive to the depreciation of its currency and to international conditions.

Warning thresholds breached

Despite the improvement in the debt-to-GDP ratio, some indicators show that Ethiopia remains at high risk. The "external debt / exports" ratio is estimated at 179.8% according to a report for 2024, well above the 150% threshold used in sustainability analyses.

The "external debt service / exports" ratio was estimated at 11.3% for 2023/24, above the 10% threshold. Debt service (interest plus principal) remains highly exposed to weak export earnings and shrinking foreign-currency resources.

These elements show that, although "dependence" in the sense of the debt-to-GDP ratio is lower, the country remains highly vulnerable to external shocks (currency, interest rates, exports) that can place heavy constraints on its finances.

The weighing factors

  • Currency depreciation and exchange-rate risk: The floating of the birr, combined with high inflation, increases the burden of external debt in local currency.
  • Weak export earnings: Ethiopia depends heavily on a few products (notably coffee) and suffers from a chronic trade deficit, which reduces its ability to repay its debt in foreign currency.
  • High investment needs: The country is seeking to close its infrastructure and development gap through borrowing, which heightens its sensitivity to financing conditions.
  • Debt suspension/renegotiation: Ethiopia has entered the restructuring framework provided by the Paris Club/G20, which has temporarily slowed new external disbursements.

What are the prospects?

In the short and medium term, several scenarios emerge. If the situation remains stable, the decline in the share of external debt in GDP could continue, improving the external dependence profile.

However, a reversal is possible: the IMF forecasts that the external debt-to-GDP ratio could climb back to 21.8% in 2025, owing to large principal repayments (about $3 billion) and lower disbursements.

It will be crucial to strengthen export earnings, stabilise the exchange rate and limit new non-concessional borrowing to avoid a fresh rebound in dependence.

The implementation of an economic reform programme (revenue mobilisation, investment efficiency, improved governance) will be decisive in reducing not only the ratio but also the associated risk.

Ethiopia is managing to reduce its external financial dependence as a proportion of GDP, but the picture remains marked by structural fragilities. Even if the overall indicator is improving, the ratios tied to exports and debt service signal that the nation remains exposed to an external shock. The real question is therefore not just "how much?", but "under what conditions?".

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4472:
Monrovia, 6 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA— The Republic of Liberia, founded in West Africa, has a singular political trajectory: its very early birth as an independent state, a long period of domination by a so-called "Americo-Liberian" elite, followed by a radical overthrow with devastating civil wars, and then a return to democratic elections. This article traces that history from independence to the present day.

From colony to independence (1822-1847)

Liberia has its roots in the initiative of the American Colonization Society (ACS), which, as early as 1816, advocated the "return" of free African Americans to Africa. In 1822, the first groups of African Americans arrived on the West African coast in what would become Liberia. On 26 July 1847, the declaration of independence of the Republic of Liberia was adopted.

Liberia then adopted a constitution modeled on that of the United States, and elected Joseph Jenkins Roberts as its first president. Thus, unlike most African states, Liberia did not go through the classic stages of European colonization followed by decolonization: it proclaimed itself independent very early, in a unique context.

Americo-Liberian hegemony and apparent stability (1847-1970)

After independence, a group of African American emigrants and their descendants, the Americo-Liberians, dominated the country's political and economic apparatus. The dominant party for a long time was the True Whig Party, which controlled the presidency and government for much of the 20th century. The country enjoyed relative formal stability and international recognition, while depending heavily on exports of rubber, iron ore and other commodities.

Nevertheless, this stability was partly superficial: power was concentrated in the hands of a minority (Americo-Liberians), while indigenous populations had limited access to senior posts, and even to the right to vote until belated reforms.

The turning point of 1980 and the fall of the old order

A major turning point came on 12 April 1980: a coup led by Samuel K. Doe, then a master sergeant of Krahn origin, ended Americo-Liberian domination and the regime of William R. Tolbert Jr. Doe became head of state through the "People's Redemption Council," initiating a new political order marked by militarization and ethnic tensions. In 1986, a new constitution was adopted and multiparty elections were held, although they were contested.

The civil wars (1989-2003)

Liberia plunged into a period of major conflict. In December 1989, the rebellion of the National Patriotic Front of Liberia (NPFL), led by Charles Taylor, launched an insurgency against Doe's regime. The conflict lasted until 1997, causing hundreds of thousands of deaths, mass displacement and the partial collapse of the Liberian state.

After Charles Taylor's election in 1997, a second civil war broke out, before the conflict ended in 2003 with Taylor's exile and the establishment of a transitional government.

Toward reconstruction and renewed democracy (2003-2025)

The post-war period marks a turning point. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (Liberia) was created in 2005 to investigate abuses during the conflicts and to recommend institutional reforms. In November 2005, Ellen Johnson Sirleaf was elected president, becoming the first woman head of state in Africa. She focused on reconstruction, debt and international relations.

In 2018, the election of George Weah was hailed as Liberia's first peaceful transfer of power since 1944. In 2024, Joseph Boakai was sworn in as president, marking a new stage.

Challenges and outlook

Despite progress, several challenges persist. The consolidation of the rule of law and democratic governance remains fragile after decades of war. The trauma of the civil wars and questions of transitional justice (for example, the establishment of a war crimes court in 2024) have yet to be addressed. Liberia's economy must overcome dependence on raw materials, a weak public sector, and a need for infrastructure and human capital. The memory of the divide between Americo-Liberians and indigenous populations continues to influence social and political dynamics.

Liberia's political history is that of a highly atypical trajectory: an African state created by free African Americans, which declared its independence as early as 1847. For more than a century it experienced elite domination, before a coup in 1980 triggered years of civil war. Since the 2000s, the country has been attempting a return to democracy, peace and reconstruction, even though the challenges remain heavy. Liberia thus embodies both the potential and the fragilities of a nation-state in Africa: rich in its unique history, but faced with the need to turn that history into stability and sustainable development.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4468:
Abuja, 6 November 2025 —PRESS AFRICA— Fifty years after its creation, the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) is going through one of the most critical periods of its existence. Born in 1975 with the promise of regional integration based on solidarity, free movement and peace, the organisation today struggles to maintain its unity in the face of political and geopolitical upheaval in the region.

A community losing cohesion

The recent withdrawals of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, made official in 2024, have deeply shaken the institution. These three countries, now united in the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), accuse ECOWAS of having become an instrument of foreign interference, too far removed from African realities. This rift marks an unprecedented break in the history of the community, which was founded precisely on the idea of a common West African destiny.

Contested sanctions and weakened leadership

The sanctions imposed on the sub-region's military regimes have crystallised criticism. While ECOWAS wanted to defend democratic principles, its economic measures have often penalised populations more than the leaders targeted. In several countries, voices are being raised to denounce an institution that is "disconnected" and "partial".

Internal divisions also weaken its authority. Between Nigeria's economic priorities, Ghana's diplomatic ambitions and Senegal's caution, it is hard to impose a common line. ECOWAS thus struggles to speak with one voice on major issues, from terrorism to regional trade.

Economic integration at a standstill

Economically, the ambition of a common market is struggling to materialise. Despite decades of discussion, the regional single currency, the ECO, remains at the project stage. Borders remain obstacles to trade, bureaucracy hampers the movement of goods, and development inequalities between member states complicate any harmonisation.

The promise of economic integration based on the free movement of people and capital now seems compromised by the return of protectionism and political tensions.

Security: a challenge that goes beyond states

On security, ECOWAS faces a succession of crises that imperil its credibility. From the jihadist threat in the Sahel to instability in Guinea and Sierra Leone, the region remains one of the most exposed on the continent.

The ECOWAS Standby Force, created precisely to respond quickly to regional threats, remains barely operational for lack of logistical means and political coordination. External interventions, whether African or international, tend to replace regional action, relegating ECOWAS to an advisory role.

A necessary overhaul

Faced with this situation, several analysts are calling for a deep overhaul of the organisation. For Ivorian political scientist Yao Kouassi, "ECOWAS must once again become a community of peoples, not just a conference of heads of state." He argues for a refocusing on regional priorities: youth employment, food security and infrastructure development.

Other observers believe ECOWAS should draw inspiration from the model of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), favouring concrete, measurable economic projects over political declarations.

An institution at a crossroads

At a time when West Africa is redefining itself politically and geostrategically, ECOWAS finds itself at a crossroads. Its survival will depend on its ability to reinvent itself, to restore the confidence of its members and to reconnect with the aspirations of West African citizens. For more than a simple regional organisation, ECOWAS remains the symbol of an ideal: that of a united and sovereign West Africa. It remains to be seen whether that ideal can still be realised.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4457:
Dar es Salaam, 6 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA— The East African country is going through a moment of crisis. Barely had the provisional results of the 29 October general election been unveiled — an official score indicating a victory for President Samia Suluhu Hassan with 97.66% — than the protests turned into clashes, urban violence and repression.

Samia Suluhu Hassan, President of Tanzania

Results, protest and social explosion

The announced victory of President Hassan, the candidate of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party, was marked by the absence from the starting line of two of the main opponents — Tundu Lissu of the opposition and Luhaga Mpina of ACT-Wazalendo — which immediately raised questions about the legitimacy of the electoral process.

From the day after the vote, protests broke out in several cities, including the economic capital, Dar es Salaam. Protesters there denounced a "sham vote", a facade of democracy and the elimination of any real competition.

Repression, curfew and internet shutdowns

To deal with the protests, the authorities imposed emergency measures: a night-time curfew in major urban areas, a nationwide cut in internet access, including to entertainment and social platforms, massive deployments of law enforcement — police and army — and the firing of tear gas and live rounds.

Human rights organisations point to a disproportionate use of force, noting that official figures remain unclear. Human Rights Watch speaks of potentially hundreds of deaths, although the government acknowledges "no official figure".

A human and social toll that is still uncertain

The main opposition parties claim that several hundred, even more than 700, people died in the violence, while United Nations sources speak of at least ten confirmed deaths.

In residential neighbourhoods as in the countryside, panicked residents describe shots fired at point-blank range, scenes of lifeless bodies, hasty burials and pressure to keep quiet.

The informal economy, vital for a large part of the Tanzanian population, has been badly hit: disrupted markets, closed shops, empty petrol stations, suspended public transport.

A legitimacy in question

President Hassan's swearing-in ceremony was held on Monday 3 November before a restricted audience, amid persistent insecurity and a heavy military presence.

The combination of an extremely high election result and the absence of genuine opponents raises serious doubts about democratic competition in Tanzania. Several regional observers consider that the vote does not meet international standards.

What prospects?

Tanzania is today at a turning point. On one side, the regime holds power and says it wants to "restore order". On the other, part of society expresses its disillusionment, its sense of injustice and a fear of arbitrary rule.

The coming weeks will be crucial: how the authorities handle the protests, the calls for an inquiry into the deaths, and the restoration of freedoms (notably of information) could either calm or further radicalise the situation. For now, Tanzanians fear a spiral of violence, both silent and plainly visible, and live daily with the rift between the institutional facade and the realities on the ground.

Reporter: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4456:
Addis Ababa, 6 November 2025 – PRESS AFRICA – Which is Africa's best-performing airline in 2025? Several international rankings help answer that question, notably those of Skytrax and AirlineRatings.com. Here is an overview of the big winners, the criteria used, and the outlook for the region.

According to Skytrax, the following airlines top the "Best Airlines in Africa" ranking for 2025:

  1. 1st: Ethiopian Airlines (Ethiopia) – for the eighth consecutive year.
  2. 2nd: Air Mauritius (Mauritius) – recognised for its quality of service and long-haul coverage.
  3. 3rd: RwandAir (Rwanda) – winner of the "Best Regional Airline in Africa" award.
  4. South African Airways (South Africa)
  5. EgyptAir (Egypt)
  6. Royal Air Maroc (Morocco)
  7. Kenya Airways (Kenya)
  8. FlySafair (South Africa, low-cost)
  9. LIFT (South Africa, low-cost)
  10. Fastjet (East Africa)

The criteria taken into account

The rankings combine several dimensions:

  • Passenger satisfaction (quality of in-flight service, comfort, entertainment). For example, Ethiopian Airlines won "Best Economy Class".
  • The destination network and the modernity of the fleet. A well-connected airline with recent aircraft scores points.
  • Operational efficiency, punctuality, cleanliness and the overall experience. For example, Airlink was named "Cleanest Airline in Africa".
  • Positioning (full-service vs low-cost): some rankings distinguish specific "Low-Cost" categories.

Strengths

Ethiopian Airlines clearly stands out for its consistency and its "pan-African" strategy: a vast network, a modern fleet and an award-winning service. Air Mauritius proves that a small island country can aim for excellence by combining high-end service with an international network. RwandAir has established itself in the regional category, which demonstrates the rising momentum of African medium-haul carriers.

Challenges

Competition remains tough: improving punctuality, spreading comfort standards more widely, and strengthening intra-African connectivity. African airlines must also contend with high costs (fuel, maintenance, infrastructure) and networks that are sometimes less densely populated. For low-cost carriers, the challenge is to maintain an acceptable quality of service while keeping fares attractive.

Outlook for travellers and the region

For a passenger based in Africa or travelling to or from Africa, favouring a highly rated airline such as Ethiopian, Air Mauritius or RwandAir can improve the experience (comfort, network, service).

For the region, this ranking is a positive sign: it indicates that African airlines can compete on the international stage. However, a real qualitative leap also requires improved airport infrastructure, staff training and regional cooperation.

In 2025, the hierarchy of African airlines is fairly clear: Ethiopian Airlines remains the undisputed leader, followed by Air Mauritius and RwandAir. However, the landscape remains fluid. New carriers may emerge, and travellers should keep an eye on the overall experience, not just the airline's name. The challenge for the whole of Africa is to turn good airlines into a concrete asset for the continent.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4451:
N'Djamena, 6 November 2025 —PRESS AFRICA— The latest Mo Ibrahim Foundation report on governance in Africa once again places Chad among the lowest-rated countries on the continent. With an overall score of 34.8 out of 100, the country ranks 47th out of 54 African states, far behind the regional average.

Chad is once again among the lowest-ranked countries in the 2025 Mo Ibrahim Index of African Governance. Despite some reforms, corruption, insecurity and the centralization of power continue to hold back progress.

A low score despite announced reforms

Chad is struggling to improve its image on the African continent. According to the latest Mo Ibrahim Foundation report, published in late October 2025, the country obtains an overall score of 34.8 out of 100, ranking 47th out of 54. The result confirms the fragility of the Chadian state in terms of governance, despite several reform announcements. "Chad illustrates the challenges Sahelian states face in reconciling stability, security and democratic governance," says an expert at the Mo Ibrahim Foundation.

Governance still too centralized

The Mo Ibrahim Index rates African countries' performance out of 100 points across four pillars. On security and the rule of law, Chad scores 28.2. On participation, rights and inclusion, it manages just 31.4 points. For economic opportunity, the country is rated at 37.5, and for human development it earns 42 points. While progress is noted in economic management, Chad remains undermined by the centralization of power, persistent corruption and tensions in peripheral regions, notably in Tibesti and the Lake Chad basin.

Timid progress over ten years

Between 2013 and 2024, Chad's overall score rose by only 3.7 points, from 31.1 to 34.8. The marginal improvement is mainly due to macroeconomic stabilization and a few public governance initiatives. "The reforms remain very concentrated in N'Djamena. In the provinces, citizens do not feel their effects," stresses Mahamat Ali, a researcher at the Sahel Center for Strategic Studies.

Regional comparison: Central Africa lags behind

Gabon, better rated in 2024 (47.6% out of 100), ranks 26th on the continent with stability over the past decade, followed by Cameroon, which totals 39.9 for 39th place with a trend of 1.5. Over the same 2013-2024 period, Congo-Brazzaville has a score of 38.6, ranking 42nd with a trend of -0.7. The Central African Republic takes 45th place with an average of 36.2 and a trend of 2.1 over the past 10 years. Chad's 34.8 points earned it 47th place with a trend of 3.7 over 10 years. Equatorial Guinea follows in 49th place with an average of 33.9 and a trend of 0.9. This picture illustrates the poor position of Central Africa, where governance remains the weak link in economic and social development.

Positive signals, but limited

The Chadian government is trying to polish its image. In October 2025, 114 public officials were trained and certified in financial management and auditing. With a view to better controlling public spending, the partnership with the African Development Bank (AfDB) has been strengthened. A revision of the transparency code is announced for 2026.

What levers for a lasting recovery?

Chad nonetheless has assets, notably a majority-young and dynamic population, underused agricultural and energy potential, and growing international cooperation (AfDB, UNDP, European Union). However, without effective decentralization and a real fight against corruption, these assets risk remaining theoretical.

In Chad, governing is no longer enough; the country must now govern better. The Mo Ibrahim Foundation's 2025 report confirms the diagnosis: Chadian governance remains behind, held back by corruption, centralization and insecurity. Despite a slight improvement, Chad remains in the bottom quarter of the continent. To reverse the trend, reforms will now have to translate into citizens' daily lives, not just in official reports.

Writer: Saïd TESSILIMI
en.4410:
Cairo, November 2, 2025—PRESS AFRICA—The 35th edition of the Africa Cup of Nations, scheduled to take place in Morocco from December 21, 2025, to January 18, 2026, is shaping up to be one of the most competitive in recent years. Among the 24 competing nations, some stand out as favorites. Here is an overview of the teams to watch.

Morocco

They arrive with strong arguments: a deep squad including players from top European leagues, home advantage, and a stated ambition to win a second continental title, with their only success dating back to 1976.

Egypt

The tournament's record-holder with seven titles, Egypt remains a reliable contender. With Mohamed Salah as the headliner and a tradition of high performance, the "Pharaohs" are aiming for an eighth crown.

Algeria

They bring together a good mix of talent and experience. They have the ambition to rise among the champions, despite a recent campaign that was not fully satisfying.

Senegal

Already victorious in 2021, Senegal combines youth and maturity. They remain a top contender thanks to their squad and their experience in major competitions.

Why Are These Teams the Favorites?

Home Advantage (Morocco): Playing at home not only offers massive popular support but also smooth logistics and familiar ground. Historically, the host nation has won the AFCON in many past editions. Quality Squads: These teams have players competing at the highest level: European clubs, the Champions League, etc. This delivers high individual and collective performance. Tournament Experience: Having previously competed in or won the AFCON provides a certain composure and invaluable experience in the final stages.

Points of Caution

Even the "giants" can stumble: AFCON is known for its surprises, unpredictable matches, and turnarounds. The "burden of being the favorite" can become a handicap: high expectations, media pressure, and fatigue from numerous competitions. The draw, injuries, or current form can alter the balance of power.

What to Watch

Morocco's journey: will they be able to handle the pressure at home and go all the way? Egypt's strong return: after some recent disappointments, can they regain their historic status? Algeria and Senegal: will they be able to live up to expectations, or will they be overwhelmed by the demands? The role of the outsiders: teams like the reigning champion Ivory Coast or other surprises could shake up the expected hierarchy.

In short, AFCON 2025 promises to be a top-level event where the favorites will have to prove they deserve their status. For fans of African football, the wait begins…

By: Roland DJESSOU
en.4398:
Nairobi, November 2, 2025—PRESS AFRICA— At the heart of East Africa, Kenya, long perceived as a model of growth, must now face a harsher social reality: poverty affects nearly 4 out of 10 Kenyans. In a context of inflation, fiscal pressure, and high debt, the poverty index reveals a worrying stagnation, and even a slight deterioration in the well-being of the society's vulnerable segments.

Persistent Data: 39.8% in 2022

The latest official survey from the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) indicates an overall poverty rate of 39.8% for the year 2022, according to the national poverty line. This threshold places more than 20 million Kenyans in a situation where they are unable to meet basic vital needs, including food, housing, health, and education.

This proportion varies across different geographical areas. In rural areas, more than 42.9% of households lived below this threshold, while in urban areas, the share was approximately 33.2%. Among these populations, hundreds of thousands were in a situation of extreme poverty.

Multidimensional Poverty: Another Face of the Challenge

Beyond income, the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) reveals that nearly a quarter, or 25.4% of the population, is considered "multidimensionally" poor—that is, simultaneously deprived of sufficient access to health, education, or decent living conditions. The national MPI is estimated at 0.113, with a relatively high intensity of deprivation in rural areas (where multidimensional poverty rates reach ~33.9%) compared to urban areas (~8.2%).

Between Hope and Setbacks: Trends and Pressures

Previous data suggested a decline in poverty between 2006 (approximately 47%) and 2019 (around 33%). But successive shocks, characterized by the COVID-19 pandemic, droughts, and global inflation, have halted this progress. In 2020, the rate rose to 42.9%, before partially decreasing in 2021 to 38.6% and then stagnating in 2022 at 39.8%.

For 2025, the outlook is mixed: although economic growth is maintained, albeit moderate, risks remain, particularly the high cost of debt, which constrains the scope for social policies. The need to create decent jobs and strengthen social safety nets is more urgent than ever.

Poverty affects nearly 40% of the Kenyan population according to the national line—a level that has stagnated after years of progress. The challenge is twofold: monetary poverty and multidimensional poverty (access to education, health, water, housing). The transition towards a sustainable reduction in poverty requires strategic investments in employment, resilient agriculture, education, and social protection.

By: Jaurès BOKO
en.4382:
Libreville, November 3, 2025—PRESS AFRICA— In a country long dominated by oil, forestry, and mining exploitation, culture is progressively emerging as an economic and identity lever in Gabon. In 2025, as growth remains modest (≈ 2.9% in 2024) and more than a third of the population lives below the poverty line, the promotion of cultural heritage, arts, and tourism is beginning to find its place in the national diversification strategy.

A Sector in Search of Recognition

While precise figures for the "culture" sector's isolated contribution to Gabon's GDP are not yet available, several observations converge. Gabon, rich in forests, traditions, and biodiversity, possesses significant cultural potential to be leveraged, notably through ecotourism, the protection of intangible heritage, and the creative industries. The country is increasingly emphasizing economic diversification and identifies ecotourism, agro-industry, technology, and, implicitly, culture among the sectors with high potential. The formalization of culture as an economic factor still remains embryonic: few studies specify the share of arts, live performance, crafts, or museums in the GDP, which limits analysis but also highlights the room for growth.

Challenges and Opportunities

Culture presents several assets for the Gabonese economy. In the context of job and activity creation, museums, festivals, crafts, performances, and cultural tourism can generate local employment, particularly in peripheral or rural areas. Regarding international influence, Gabon can promote its heritage (indigenous peoples, traditions, biodiversity, contemporary art) to attract visitors and investors, thereby improving the country's image. As for economic diversification, at a time when 97% of Gabonese exports come from oil, wood, and manganese, according to 2024 data, culture constitutes a vehicle for diversification. In any case, a synergy with the natural sectors is urgently needed. Cultural heritage is often linked to natural resources (forests, national parks, indigenous art); leveraging this combination opens up paths for a joint green and cultural economy.

Hurdles to Overcome

Several obstacles currently hinder the emergence of culture as an economic driver in Gabon. These include, among others, the lack of statistics: the absence of reliable indicators for culture's share of the GDP or for the arts and creation sector limits the sector's visibility; the lack of an institutional framework and funding: cultural institutions and entrepreneurs often lack support, dedicated financing, and training to structure economically viable projects; the dependence on natural resources: the Gabonese economy remains heavily dependent on oil and the export of raw materials, which reduces the relative appeal of sectors with higher cultural or creative intensity; and insufficient infrastructure to support logistics: cultural tourism or artistic events require infrastructure (accommodation, transport, communication) that the country still needs to strengthen.

Outlook for 2026-2030

The Gabonese government, as part of its post-transition development plan, intends to strengthen the digital economy, agro-industry, tourism, and, by extension, culture. The challenges will notably be to further integrate culture into national development strategies; to allocate specific resources (funds, incentives, training) to the creative industries; and to strengthen international partnerships to promote cultural heritage and support local actors.

In 2025, culture in Gabon is not yet a major, measurable pillar of the economy, but it is beginning to establish itself as an essential element of the national diversification and identity strategy. If the right conditions are met—funding, data, infrastructure, framework—the sector could become a driver of inclusive growth and influence for the country.

By: Jaurès BOKO
en.4360:
Brazzaville, November 1, 2025—PRESS AFRICA— In the Central African sub-region, the labor market is at a crossroads. While some countries report relatively moderate unemployment rates, others like the Republic of Congo or Gabon show very high levels, reflecting marked structural weaknesses in employment, training, and the informal economy.

A Few Recent Indicators

In 2024, the Central African Republic recorded an unemployment rate of approximately 5.9% of the active population. In Congo-Brazzaville, the rate was estimated at 19.8% in 2024, down from 20.1% in 2023. For the central region as a whole, a study by the Economic Commission for Africa indicated that in 2022, states like Gabon and the Republic of Congo showed rates "well above" the regional average. These figures, however, hide major differences based on age, gender, and level of education: the 2022 study showed that youth unemployment reached 16.6%, compared to about 9.8% for the general active population.

Why Such Disparities?

Several factors explain this situation. There is a very prominent informal economy: in many countries of the sub-region, a large portion of jobs is not recorded in formal statistics; this can skew the "official" unemployment rates. There is also the dependence on raw materials: several Central African economies rely heavily on oil, wood, or minerals. In the event of an external shock, formal jobs falter. Another factor remains the weakness of industry and the structured tertiary sector: the lack of stable jobs in manufacturing or formalized services pushes a part of the population into the informal sector. Also noteworthy is the mismatch between training and employment: the education and vocational training system struggles to produce the skills required by employers in the sub-region. Furthermore, young people and women are more vulnerable: unemployment more heavily affects the youth and women, which worsens inequalities in the labor market.

Economic and Social Consequences

High unemployment or long-term precarious employment lead to, among other things, a loss of income for many families, reducing domestic savings and investment capacity; an increased reliance on the informal sector, which limits contributions and weakens social protection; social and political instability, as high youth unemployment rates create a risk of frustration, migration, or even tensions; and reduced room for maneuver for public policies, as tax revenues remain low and social budgets are constrained.

Some Avenues for Improvement

To reverse this trend, certain strategies appear useful. These include strengthening professional and technical training, in alignment with the needs of growth sectors (digital, agro-industry, services); promoting the formalization of employment and supporting micro-enterprises / SMEs to expand the supply of stable jobs; developing economic diversification by reducing dependence on raw materials and promoting labor-intensive sectors; implementing targeted policies for young people and women to reduce disparities and increase inclusion; and improving the collection of reliable data on the labor market, which would allow for better-targeted employment policies.

The employment situation in Central Africa in 2025 reveals stark contrasts: some countries seem to have their labor market under control, while others remain caught in cycles of high unemployment and persistent informality. The challenge is not only economic but also social: for growth to translate into quality jobs, political will, structural reforms, and a dynamic public-private partnership are essential.

Editor: Jaurès BOKO
en.4359:
Ouagadougou, 03 November—PRESS AFRICA— The Burkinabe economy is characterized by a croissance of 3.8¨% of GDP that prevents a strong resistance, in a context of security tenduity and political mutation. Malgré les crises régionales, la croissance du pais reste positive, générée par l’agriculture, l’or et le secteur informal. Mais derrière ces signaux encouragingants, les faiblesses structurelles demeurent important.

The Strengths of a Resilient Economy

Two sectors in particular—a vital agricultural industry and a foundational gold sector—combined with an enterprising youth, currently form the strength of the Burkinabé economy.

Agriculture, which accounts for 30% of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP), remains the economic heart of Burkina Faso, employing nearly 80% of the active population. Cotton, maize, millet, and sesame are key export pillars. Despite climate-related challenges, reforms in the cotton industry and the promotion of resilient crops have supported production and rural incomes.

As the second-largest gold producer in West Africa, Burkina Faso derives nearly 75% of its export revenue from the precious metal. In 2025, rising global gold prices and the modernization of certain mines helped stabilize public revenue, despite the closure of some sites for security reasons.

With an average age of 17, the country has considerable demographic potential. Young people under 25 make up 65% of the population. This youth demographic is increasingly venturing into the digital, agri-food, and local commerce sectors. Microfinance and business incubator programs are tentatively supporting this entrepreneurial drive.

Structural Weaknesses to Overcome

Overall, the challenging security context, excessive dependence on gold and agriculture, and still-high poverty levels are the weaknesses of the Burkinabé economy.

For several years, attacks in the northern and eastern parts of the country have disrupted trade and agricultural supply chains, leading to massive population displacement and a slowdown in investment. This factor remains the primary obstacle to sustainable growth.

The Burkinabé economy remains poorly diversified. Revenue from gold and cotton is vulnerable to international price fluctuations. A lack of industrialization and infrastructure limits local processing and thus the creation of stable jobs.

In 2025, over 35% of Burkinabè citizens live below the national poverty line. Access to electricity, clean water, and education remains unequal across regions. The informal sector, which accounts for over 90% of employment, reflects both the vitality and the precarity of the economy.

Outlook for 2026

Regional institutions forecast a growth of 4.5% for 2026, supported by an agricultural recovery and public investment.
However, political stability, security, and economic diversification remain essential conditions for transforming this growth into inclusive development.

By: Jaurès BOKO
en.4329:
Malabo, 2 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA— In 2025, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) remain the backbone of African economies; they create jobs and local innovation and form links in regional value chains. As public policy and donors seek to close the vast gap in financing and infrastructure, certain sectors stand out as particularly promising for SMEs: they combine growing demand, relatively low barriers to entry and opportunities to move up the value chain. A tour of the opportunities to seize.

Agri-food and agro-processing

Agri-food remains the most logical option for many African SMEs: processing raw materials locally (cereals, fruit, dairy products) creates added value, reduces imports and meets fast-growing domestic and regional demand. SMEs that specialise in preservation, packaging, cold logistics and climate-resilient farm inputs are finding stable outlets, notably through short supply chains, local markets and regional exports. Targeted value-chain financing and technical support (standards, certifications) are decisive levers.

Renewable energy

The rise of decentralised solar, mini-grids and storage solutions opens up a broad field for SMEs: installation, maintenance, local manufacturing of simple components, financing of pay-as-you-go appliances and energy-efficiency services. The potential is twofold: serving the 600 million people still without electricity and providing cheaper, more reliable energy to businesses. The green transition also stimulates opportunities in light electric mobility and sustainable construction. Reports show that the "green economy" could generate millions of jobs if training and financing are brought together.

FinTech, digitalisation and business services

African SMEs benefit from a dynamic FinTech ecosystem (mobile payments, digital micro-credit, parametric insurance) that reduces transaction costs and eases access to customers. At the same time, demand for digital services (e-commerce, urban logistics, digital marketing, B2B platforms) continues to explode. SMEs that offer "mobile-first" solutions and management tools adapted to local realities can very quickly excel nationally and regionally. Support from international financial institutions and SME competitiveness programmes is accelerating this transition.

Health and local pharmaceutical production

The pandemic exposed the vulnerability of health supply chains. SMEs entering the manufacture of simple APIs, local production of protective equipment, pharmaceutical distribution, rapid diagnostics and home-care services are finding an expanding market. Investment in skills, regulatory compliance and public-private partnerships is, however, essential to turn this opportunity into sustainable growth.

Education, vocational training and EdTech

Demand for vocational training, upskilling and distance-learning solutions remains very high, driven by a young population and the growing needs of labour markets. EdTech SMEs offering content tailored to sought-after skills (technical, green, digital) have a significant competitive advantage, especially if they work with employers and certification bodies.

Sustainable tourism, culture and the creative economy

Despite cyclical shocks (security, pandemics), sustainable tourism and the creative economy (fashion, music, digital content) offer high margins and international visibility. SMEs that position themselves on local experience, responsible hospitality or the export of digital cultural goods can earn foreign currency and create skilled jobs.

Obstacles and recommendations…

The main obstacle remains financing: African SMEs face a large credit gap, high borrowing costs and collateral that is hard to muster. The findings of several international institutions show that suitable instruments (leasing, factoring, partial guarantees, targeted grants) and better infrastructure (energy, roads, logistics) are priorities. Other levers include strengthening management capacity, access to regional markets through free trade areas, and easing regulatory procedures.

For entrepreneurs and investors, the opportunities are real and varied in 2025: agro-processing, solar, digital, health, EdTech and sustainable tourism stand out as sectors where SMEs can grow rapidly and create jobs. Turning these opportunities into large-scale success will, however, require a combination of patient capital, technical support and favourable public policy.

Writer: Khadidjatou BAWA ALLAH
en.4316:
Johannesburg, 2 November 2025—PRESS AFRICA— In 2025, Africa is facing a worrying reality: the use of and dependence on psychoactive substances among young people has emerged as a major public health problem, with marked variations by region, substance and social vulnerability.

According to recently published reports and scientific reviews, substance use among adolescents and young adults in sub-Saharan Africa remains high and uneven: alcohol, tobacco and cannabis remain the most widely used substances, while the non-medical use of opioids (notably tramadol) and the arrival of powerful synthetic narcotics (nitazenes) are rising rapidly in several countries in West and Central Africa. These new substances, sometimes mixed with traditional drugs, expose young people to increased risks of overdose and health complications.

The available figures vary widely between studies and countries, but recent epidemiological reviews estimate that in some areas the prevalence of use of at least one substance among adolescents can reach 30–45%. Rates are generally higher in disadvantaged urban settings, among out-of-school youth and those exposed to conflict or high unemployment. Moreover, access to treatment services remains dramatically low: Africa has one of the lowest rates of treatment coverage for substance use disorders in the world, leaving the majority of young people without appropriate care.

Several structural factors explain this situation. Weak mental health and addiction care systems, social stigma, the absence of suitable school prevention programmes, and a growing illegal supply — linked to the rise of trafficking corridors and the mixing of local and international markets — contribute to young people's increased exposure. To this are added cultural and economic factors: recreational alcohol use, easy access to illicitly sold opioid medicines (tramadol), self-medication practices and psychosocial pressures.

Local examples show the scale of the human challenge: in some countries in southern and western Africa, local organisations report dangerous practices (injections, consumption of unknown mixtures, "kush" mixed with synthetics) that have already led to overdoses and an increase in communicable infections. These phenomena are pushing mothers, neighbourhood associations and NGOs to launch education campaigns and psychosocial support units, often with limited means.

At the regional level, specific dynamics can be observed. In West and Central Africa, there is a rise in tramadol and the detection of nitazenes in certain mixtures, adulterated "kush" cannabis markets and growing exposure despite rudimentary chemical analysis capacity. In southern Africa, there is an increased presence of methamphetamine and injection practices in urban pockets, with a strong correlation observed between drug use and HIV-related risks in some contexts. East and North Africa are characterised by variations from country to country, but with warning signs of non-medical use of prescription drugs and of contamination routes linked to drug transit.

Policy and operational responses exist, but remain fragmentary. The African Union and international agencies have stepped up calls to action and youth-focused prevention programmes, promoting peer education, training for health personnel and the strengthening of national drug surveillance capacities. However, implementation is hampered by limited resources, competing priorities (security, humanitarian crises) and persistent stigma. Many experts are calling for a change of direction: moving from a purely repressive approach to integrated strategies combining prevention, harm reduction, treatment and social reintegration.

Promising solutions are nevertheless emerging: youth-led community interventions, evidence-based school prevention programmes, integrated mental health and addiction treatment centres, and screening and information campaigns that use social media and peer education. Improving surveillance of drug markets (chemical analysis, rapid reporting) is also crucial to quickly detect the arrival of new and dangerous substances.

In conclusion, 2025 marks a turning point: drug use among young Africans is no longer a marginal phenomenon but a multidimensional crisis that demands coordinated, funded and public-health-centred responses. Without a significant increase in prevention, treatment and harm reduction capacity, African societies risk seeing avoidable human and social losses grow. The main issue remains the political will to invest in solutions adapted to local realities and led by and for young people themselves.

Reporter: Khadidjatou BAWA ALLAH
en.4299:
Abidjan, 24 October 2025 – PRESS AFRICA – It is a rich year for African stars: amid international successes, streaming records, prestigious nominations and the expansion of their global influence, several artists, athletes and creators from the continent are taking centre stage. Here are three who embody this momentum.

Ayra Starr of Nigeria:

She is increasingly seen as "the Gen Z icon of Afrobeats". In 2025, she was the most-nominated African star at the 2025 BET Awards: three nominations, including "Best Female R&B/Pop", "Best New Artist" and "Best International Act", have put her under the global spotlight. Her album "The Year I Turned 21" dominated streaming platforms in West Africa in 2024-2025, and she is now engaged in international collaborations. Ayra Starr symbolises a new generation of African artists who are no longer content with the "local" but aim for the universal.

Tyla, the South African:

South African singer Tyla confirmed her global stature in 2025. After her hit "Water", she became the first South African artist to win a major prize at the iHeartRadio Music Awards (World Artist of the Year) and, at the American Music Awards, she took the title of "Favourite Afrobeats Artist". Tyla proves that African success is no longer confined to the continent: massive streaming, international tours, appearances at major festivals… She also embodies the growing power of Afrobeats in global pop culture.

Tems of Nigeria:

An already established artist, Tems continues to make her mark in 2025. She won a Grammy in the "Best African Music Performance" category for her track "Love Me JeJe" and consolidated her reputation as an influential voice of Afrobeats and African R&B. Beyond music, she is taking on a growing number of cross-disciplinary projects and is a link between African talent and global stages.

Why do these stars matter in 2025?

In terms of global reach: they go beyond Africa's borders, with international streaming, tours and collaborations with top artists. On the new generation and digital front, they make full use of digital platforms, TikTok and Instagram, and are redefining African identity in global pop. Beyond music, they are brands, creators and role models for young people on the continent in the fields of image and influence. Their track records are also diverse: although all three are musicians, they show that Africa no longer has a single "type" of success but several avenues (fashion, multimedia, international collaboration).

The influence of these celebrities also raises important questions. What about the management of their image, the capture of value for their home countries, their social impact? The role of African stars is evolving. They are no longer merely "representatives" but potentially agents of change.

The Top 10 African stars in 2025

1. Tyla (South Africa) – Global singer of the year: after her worldwide hit "Water", Tyla consolidated her fame with a sold-out world tour and a historic win at the 2025 American Music Awards. She has become a global ambassador for African pop and the amapiano style, inspiring an entire generation of young artists.

2. Ayra Starr (Nigeria) – Gen Z icon of Afrobeats: three nominations at the 2025 BET Awards and collaborations with American stars (SZA, Chris Brown). She embodies the feminisation of African musical leadership and Nigeria's cultural power on the world stage.

3. Tems (Nigeria) – Golden voice and symbol of excellence: 2025 Grammy winner for "Best African Music Performance" with Love Me JeJe. She is stepping up charitable initiatives in West Africa and promotes an image of authenticity and female empowerment.

4. Burna Boy (Nigeria) – Ambassador of the continent: in 2025, he celebrated passing the billion-stream mark on Spotify and remains one of the highest-paid African artists in the world. He has also launched a foundation for African youth, focused on culture and entrepreneurship.

5. Asisat Oshoala (Nigeria) – Icon of African women's football: the Nigerian striker, a star of FC Barcelona Femení, won her sixth African Women's Player of the Year award. She is an active campaigner for the recognition and funding of women's sport on the continent.

6. Wizkid (Nigeria) – The musical strategist: still a headliner, Wizkid released a critically acclaimed album with hybrid Afro-Latin sounds in 2025. He remains an essential reference in the global Afrobeats industry.

7. Black Sherif (Ghana) – The African hip-hop revelation: with his album The Villain I Never Was II, he has conquered the English-speaking African market and performed on Europe's biggest stages. He symbolises the rise of conscious African hip-hop, rooted in the continent's social reality.

8. Trevor Noah (South Africa) – Voice of African humour and lucidity: the former host of The Daily Show continues an international stand-up career, with his Born a Lion tour in 2025. He remains an emblematic figure of an unapologetic African voice facing the West.

9. Angelique Kidjo (Benin) – The eternal legend: in 2025, she celebrated 40 years of career with a monumental concert in Cotonou and a world tour, "Mother of Sound". Still committed, she champions the cause of girls and education in Africa through her Batonga Foundation.

10. Mohamed Salah (Egypt) – The pharaoh of football: a star of Liverpool FC, Salah remains a model of humility and sporting excellence. In 2025, he passed the 250-goal mark in his European career, consolidating his status as a living legend of African sport.

These ten personalities embody a modern, bold and creative Africa, proud of its roots but turned towards the world. Their success is no longer limited to the continent's borders: they shape global trends, redefine the image of Africa and inspire a new generation.

Writer: Jaurès BOKO
en.4296:
Sèmè, 29 October 2025—PRESS AFRIKA— After nearly three decades of shutdown, the Sèmè field (Block 1) off the coast of Benin is once again at the center of attention: drilling campaigns have resumed, production units have been contracted and the country is seriously considering relaunching commercial production by the end of 2025. Recent developments confirm both the existence of recoverable resources and the concrete possibility of production in the short term.

Field and reserves

The Sèmè field is located in Block 1 (Dahomey Basin), in shallow waters (20-30 m). The block covers about 551 km² and includes the field discovered in the late 1960s, which was already produced between 1982 and 1998. Recent studies and independent expert reports have confirmed significant residual volumes in several reservoirs (H6, H7, H8), making it economically feasible to bring it back into production through modern rehabilitation.

Production targets
