The operators have planned a phased restart of production, namely a drilling campaign (three wells scheduled), and the installation of a mobile offshore production unit (MOPU) and a storage system (FSO). Officials announce initial production targeted for the fourth quarter of 2025, with a starting flow rate expected at around 15,000 barrels per day.

The blocks under review

Block 1 (Sèmè Field) is located in the coastal zone. It is the historic block containing the Sèmè field, for which the operator Akrake (a group linked to Rex/Lime) holds a 76% operator interest; the Beninese state retains about 15% and Octogone Trading/Octogone E&P holds about 9%. There are also the contiguous blocks (2, 3, 4, ...) of the coastal strip and the continental shelf of the Dahomey Basin, which have been divided into several exploration blocks of varying coverage: larger blocks offshore, smaller blocks close to the coast. Geological studies (paleostratigraphy, 2D/3D seismic) show additional potential but require drilling and new data to confirm exploitable volumes.

The Beninese state holds a 15% stake through the production sharing contract (PSC) and is the counterpart for fiscal, regulatory and environmental structuring. Service providers (MOPU, FSO, lifting companies, seismic and geotechnical contractors) and logistics shipowners also play a key role. Several MOPU/FSO contracts were signed or finalized during 2025.

Economic, technical and environmental stakes

Scale and profitability: the volumes already produced historically, some 22 million barrels between 1982 and 1998, and current estimates make the project viable on a small to medium scale if drilling, installation and logistics costs remain under control. The MOPU/FSO approach is precisely aimed at reducing CAPEX.

Governance and revenue: transparent management of revenue, and clear rules on local employment, procurement and taxation, will be decisive in turning the resource into benefits for the Beninese people.

Environment and safety: offshore activities require pollution prevention plans, emissions monitoring, waste management and emergency response provisions, all elements to be built into contracts and public oversight.

Sustainability and diversification: even if the restart is promising, Benin must use these resources to finance economic diversification (infrastructure, education, renewable energy) in order to avoid excessive dependence on hydrocarbons.

The existing technical and contractual elements show that the existence of oil in Benin is no longer a hypothesis: the Sèmè field is confirmed, drilling and equipment work is under way and production is plausible in the short term. However, turning this opportunity into an engine of sustainable development will depend heavily on Benin's ability to govern the sector, negotiate favorable contracts and invest the revenue strategically.

Writer: Khadidjatou BAWA ALLAH
en.4293:
Conakry, 27 October 2025—PRESS AFRIKA— As trade between Africa and China gathers pace, Guinea stands out as one of the main suppliers of strategic raw materials to Chinese industry.

A key position in raw materials

Several analyses indicate that Guinea plays a major role in supplying China, which imports very large quantities of minerals and raw materials from Africa: crude oil, copper, cobalt and aluminium ore. As regards aluminium and its input ore, bauxite, in particular, China depends heavily on Guinea.

What of their relationship

Several factors explain this Sino-Guinean relationship. Guinea has significant mineral resources, notably bauxite, an ore essential to the aluminium production chain. China has stepped up its mining and infrastructure investments in the country to secure these supplies. The global context is pushing China to diversify or strengthen its sources, and Guinea stands out.

Guinea's strong export relationship with China has several implications, notably: dependence and vulnerability, since China's heavy reliance on one or a few countries for imports of raw materials can pose a strategic risk; limited value added, since although Guinea exports raw materials, their transformation into higher-value products often takes place abroad; the opportunity for industrialisation, since for Guinea and similar countries this relationship can serve as a springboard to develop a local resource-processing industry in order to move up the value chain and capture more revenue; and geopolitics and diplomacy, since the extraction and export of these raw materials place the country in a strategic position vis-à-vis China, which can bring both benefits and challenges.

Resource-rich African countries must now choose between remaining exporters of raw materials and turning to local industrialisation in order to capture more value. Dependence on raw-material exports to large buyers such as China may be an advantage in the short term, but poses long-term risks if prices fall or geopolitical shifts occur. The China-Africa relationship continues to evolve: while China exports manufactured goods to Africa, it imports minerals and raw materials from Africa.

Guinea clearly illustrates how an African country can become a pillar of raw-material supply for China. This position brings significant economic opportunities, but also major challenges in terms of dependence, moving up the value chain and strategic sustainability. For Africa in general, this model raises the question of how to move from mere extraction to genuine processing and industrialisation.

Writer: Sastre KANE
en.4289:
Lagos, 26 October 2025—PRESS AFRIKA—Against a backdrop of rapidly growing trade between China and Africa, Nigeria now emerges as the continent's biggest consumer of products from Chinese industries. According to an analysis of Chinese customs data for the first half of 2025, Nigeria accounts for 11% of African imports from China, ahead of South Africa (10%) and Egypt (9%).

Rapidly growing demand

The phenomenon is part of an overall increase: African imports of Chinese products rose 25% year on year to about $122 billion over the first seven months of 2025, according to African Business.

In Nigeria, this trend translates into increased demand for a wide range of goods: phones, household appliances, vehicles, construction equipment, solar panels and more.

Why Nigeria?

Several factors explain this position. Nigeria is Africa's most populous economy (more than 200 million inhabitants) and has a fast-expanding consumer market. Access to competitively priced Chinese products meets broad needs: from the urban consumer to demand for infrastructure equipment. The penetration of Chinese brands (smartphones, household appliances) is strong in the big cities and peri-urban areas.

A structural trade imbalance

This situation is not without consequences: Nigeria imports massively from China, but its exports to China remain modest by comparison. This type of relationship illustrates a wider issue for Africa: importing high-value finished goods while remaining a supplier of raw materials.

Issues and prospects

For consumers, the Chinese offer provides access to relatively low-cost goods and greater choice. For local industry, this import dependence raises the question of the competitiveness of local manufacturers and of domestic value added. For policymakers, the challenge is to rebalance trade by promoting industrialisation and local processing, while ensuring that mass imports do not weaken national production chains; and for China itself, Africa, and Nigeria in particular, represents a growth relay and an outlet for its industries and surplus manufacturing capacity.

Nigeria today stands at a crossroads: a dynamic market for Chinese products, it also embodies the contemporary challenges of African industrial integration, between the import of finished goods and the aspiration to local industrialisation. Understanding this phenomenon also means anticipating the economic policies needed so that growth is not limited to consumption but also fosters production and value added.

Reporter: Michaël AKEKE
en.4285:
Abidjan, 25 October 2025 – PRESS AFRICA – TikTok, the Chinese video-sharing platform, has become in just a few years one of the most widely used social networks on the African continent. While it has opened the door for many talents, content creators and entrepreneurs, it is now at the centre of growing controversy: sexual excesses, suggestive content, the exploitation of minors and the normalisation of risky behaviour.

Meteoric popularity, but a double-edged sword

With more than 150 million active African users in 2025, TikTok has established itself as young people's favourite medium. In countries such as Nigeria, Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire, Kenya and South Africa, it serves as a springboard for a digital generation hungry for visibility. However, this thirst for fame often turns into a race for "buzz", and that is where the excesses appear.

Early sexualisation and the quest for virality

Investigations carried out in Nigeria, Cameroon and Senegal in 2024 show a proliferation of accounts posting videos with sexual overtones, often run by very young girls. Some are no more than 16. Viral "challenges" — dance-based, suggestive or provocative — encourage early sexualisation and normalise erotic gestures or remarks. This phenomenon, heightened by TikTok's algorithm, which rewards content that provokes strong reactions, feeds a dangerous spiral: the more shocking a piece of content is, the more widely it is shared.

The role of influencers and the commodification of the body

Many African influencers have specialised in "sexy" or suggestive content, aiming to monetise their views through product placements or live donations, the so-called "lives".

In several countries, young women use the platform to sell explicit content via external links, a practice amounting to disguised pornography, yet prohibited by the network's terms of use. This commodification of the body finds a worrying echo in contexts of economic hardship: some young girls see TikTok as a quick way to gain visibility, money or gifts from fans.

Risks for minors and the silence of the authorities

Child protection associations warn of the psychological and social consequences of this exposure. Cases of blackmail, harassment, the circulation of intimate images and online sexual exploitation have been recorded.

Yet in most African countries, the legal framework remains unclear. Cybercrime legislation does not always cover the specific protection of minors on social networks. Few awareness campaigns exist, and platforms are slow to moderate content in local languages effectively.

Shared responsibility: families, schools and platforms

African experts and sociologists stress that tackling these excesses must involve several levels. First, families, often overwhelmed by young people's digital habits, need to be trained in digital parenting. Schools, for their part, must incorporate media literacy and digital citizenship education, and platforms such as TikTok have a responsibility to strengthen moderation, particularly in Africa, where their oversight centres remain undersized.

Towards an African response to digital excess

Several African countries, such as Kenya and Morocco, have begun to consider stricter oversight of online content. Nigeria announced in 2025 the creation of a monitoring unit dedicated to social networks, while the African Union is preparing a charter on the "digital protection of minors". But without collective action — educational, legal and technological — the line between creativity and exploitation risks disappearing.

Sexual excesses on TikTok are not merely a moral or technological problem: they reflect economic inequality, a crisis of reference points and a lack of guidance for young people in several African societies. Africa, which has embraced digital technology with enthusiasm, must now learn to regulate it responsibly. The challenge is immense: protecting young people without stifling creativity.

Writer: Souleymane SYLA
en.4281:
Ouagadougou, 23 October 2025—PRESS AFRIKA— In a quarter of a century, marriage among young West Africans has changed profoundly. While in 2000 nearly seven in ten young people were married before the age of 30, the 2025 figures reveal a spectacular fall: barely a third now reach that milestone. Behind this disengagement lies a major social transformation, driven by urbanization, economic precarity and changing attitudes.

A sharp drop in young people's marriage rate

According to data compiled by the African Union and ECOWAS, the marriage rate of young people aged 18 to 30 fell from 68% in 2000 to 34% in 2025 on average across West African countries.

The trend is visible in almost every country. Today, only 38% of young Nigerians marry, compared with 70% in 2000. In Ghana, the decline is 29% (33% in 2025 against 62% in 2000). In Senegal, 30% marry in 2025, whereas in 2000, 65% of young people did. The same finding applies in Benin, where only 31% unite today against 67% 25 years ago. Côte d'Ivoire is no exception: the decline in marriages amounts to 35%, from 63% to 28%. It turns out that in 2025 Côte d'Ivoire holds the sad record for the lowest youth marriage rate in West Africa.

Experts note that the decline is sharper in urban areas, where young people now prioritize studies, financial stability and personal independence before marriage.

Studies, employment and autonomy: priorities are changing

In 2000, marriage was seen as an almost obligatory passage into adulthood. In 2025, it has become a considered choice, sometimes postponed or replaced by other forms of union. Young graduates, men and women alike, say in regional surveys that they first want to "build their lives" before committing.

This shift is also explained by rising youth unemployment, which exceeds 25% in several countries, making economic stability a prerequisite for any marriage plan.

"You can't get married without a stable career. It's not like it used to be," says Mariam, 27, an entrepreneur in Dakar.

Between traditions and new forms of union

While religious or customary marriage remains the norm in many rural regions, cohabitation and free relationships are on the rise in urban centers.

These models, long considered contrary to African values, are gradually establishing themselves as social realities. Lavish ceremonies, high dowries and the cost of living are additional obstacles: in Benin, for example, the average budget for an urban wedding exceeds 2 million CFA francs, equivalent to several months of average salary.

Women, agents of change

One of the major factors in this transformation is the growing role of women in education and employment. In 2000, fewer than one woman in four pursued higher education; in 2025, it is one in two in several French-speaking countries. Young women are now delaying the age of marriage to pursue their professional and personal ambitions.

However, this change is not unanimously welcomed: some traditionalist voices see a "crisis of family values," while others read it as a conquest of freedom and equality.

Social and cultural challenges ahead

The decline in the marriage rate has multiple repercussions, including a rise in births outside marriage in some urban settings; intergenerational tensions between modernity and custom; the reconfiguration of family structures and community solidarity; and a lifestyle model inspired by social media.

Religious and customary authorities call for a "balance between tradition and modernity," while sociologists argue for adapting family law to new social realities.

West Africa is not experiencing a "marriage crisis" but a redefinition of marriage. Young people are not rejecting the institution; they are rethinking it: more freedom, more choice, more equality. This deep sociological shift shows that in 2025, loving and uniting are no longer conceived as they were in 2000.

Writer: Ouédraogo TOURE
en.4267:
Cotonou, 22 October 2025 - PRESS AFRICA-In the bustling streets of Cotonou, an unexpected phenomenon is drawing attention: more and more older people are taking the handlebars of the famous motorbike taxis, known as zémidjan. This return to roots is redefining the codes of a trade often seen as the preserve of the young, and raises economic, social and cultural questions.

A traditional trade revisited

For several months, the taxi ranks at bus stations and the main thoroughfares of Benin's economic capital have seen a new kind of zémidjan driver reappear: men over 55, sometimes even beyond 70.

"After working all my life in trade, retirement was not easy. Coming back as a zém lets me stay active, earn a living and stay connected with society," explains Augustin, 67, on his bike near Dantokpa market.

The reasons for a return

Several factors explain the phenomenon. Among others: the economic crisis and inadequate pensions, as many elders have no stable income in retirement and must find a supplementary source of revenue; the rising cost of living, since in the face of persistent inflation the Kèkènon trade remains accessible and lucrative despite its risks; social dynamics and recognition, since the job offers a degree of autonomy, social status and direct contact with the public, often valued by these seniors; and family pressure, as some feel duty-bound to contribute to the household budget or help their children and grandchildren.

A physical and social challenge

Taking up a physically demanding trade again at an advanced age is not without challenges. Several health organisations warn of the risks linked to fatigue, accidents and harsh working conditions.

An evolving image

Long seen as a dangerous trade reserved for young men, the zémidjan is opening up to a new generational and social diversity. For Beninese sociologist Dr Koffi Hounkpe, "This return of older people to the trade reflects a profound change in attitudes to work, but also an economic necessity. It is a form of social resilience that deserves to be recognised and supported."

Young drivers, sometimes sceptical, are beginning to see these veterans as sources of advice and experience, fostering an unprecedented intergenerational dynamic. In the words of young Kèkènon Moussa, "They know the city better than we do, and we learn a lot from rubbing shoulders with them."

The return of older people to the zémidjan trade in Cotonou illustrates people's capacity to adapt to today's economic and social challenges. The phenomenon upends preconceptions, invites a rethink of urban solidarity, and lays the foundations for a more inclusive and intergenerational trade. However, it is urgent that the central government steer the socio-professional reintegration of older people who are obliged to work to meet their basic needs towards other, less risky sectors, in order to limit and/or prevent the worst.

Writer: Khadidjatou BAWA ALLAH
en.4264:
Niamey, 22 October 2025 - PRESS AFRICA - As several parts of Africa face a resurgence of terrorist activity and transnational organised crime, financing the fight against terrorism and disrupting illicit flows have become major challenges. What financing mechanisms are available, what gaps persist, and what are the prospects for making the African response more effective and lasting?

On the continent, terrorist groups and criminal organisations use a variety of funding channels: trafficking in natural resources, extortion, money laundering, ransoms and informal financial transfers. According to the United Nations Office of Counter-Terrorism (UNOCT), the link between organised crime and terrorism is a "growing concern". During a debate in the Security Council, it was noted that the illicit exploitation of natural resources plays a central role in financing armed groups in Africa. This twofold security and financial challenge requires not only military or police operations, but also financial engineering, governance and regional and international cooperation.

Gaps, challenges and obstacles

Several obstacles hamper the effectiveness of counter-terrorism financing in Africa. These include, among others, insufficient predictable and sustainable funding. In the Security Council, it was stressed that Africa was "tired of hearing promises and reaping only disappointment"; limited institutional capacity, reflected in shortcomings in training, in the oversight of financial flows and in transnational cooperation; the opacity of funding channels generated by the informal economy, non-bank transfers or trafficking in natural resources; and the failure to strengthen regional coordination. West African, Sahelian and East African states must better coordinate their compliance regimes, their financial regulations and their cross-border investigations.

Some avenues

An effective fight against terrorist financing must rely on stronger monitoring of illicit financial flows, in particular those that feed terrorism, through better banking supervision and the inclusion of non-financial actors (real estate, precious metals, etc.); robust regional coordination, drawing on institutions and sharing information between states; the mobilisation of more stable, dedicated financial resources, rather than one-off donations, to support national capacities over the long term; the integration of economic development and governance as pillars of prevention; and the involvement of civil society and private actors, because the fight against financial flows cannot rest on the state alone.

Financing the fight against terrorism in Africa is at a crossroads. On the one hand, initiatives are multiplying: donations, regional projects, international partnerships. On the other, institutional challenges, the weakness of sustainable resources and the evolving methods used by terrorist groups to raise funds demand rapid adaptation. For Africa to have a truly effective response, it will need not only funds, but also a long-term architecture capable of following the money, breaking the chains of financing and developing local means.

Reporter: Jaurès BOKO
en.4259:
Cotonou, 22 October 2025 – PRESS AFRICA – In 2025, Benin is confirming its determination to become a leading tourist destination in West Africa. Thanks to reforms, investment in infrastructure and a greater emphasis on its historical, cultural and natural heritage, the country is recording encouraging signs in the sector. What are the main trends in tourist flows, the government initiatives, the challenges and the outlook for the future?

Several assets boost the appeal of Benin as a destination. First and foremost, the country's leaders have set out a clear strategy through a five-year investment plan for the sector worth CFA 797 billion (about US$1.4 billion) to develop tourism, culture and the arts between 2025 and 2029. It aims in particular to raise tourism's share of GDP from 6% to 13.4% by 2030. Added to this are varied landscapes (beaches, lagoons, natural parks) that attract tourists in search of authenticity; a cultural and heritage wealth made up of historic sites, the Slave Route in Ouidah and Vodun traditions; and relative political stability, conducive to tourism.

Key flows and data

Although very recent detailed figures are limited, several sources point to growing tourism. In earlier years, Benin welcomed visitors to sites such as Ouidah (about 500,000 visitors a year) and Pendjari (about 200,000 visitors a year). Regional collaboration is under way: in July 2025, the Nigerian Association of Tour Operators (NATOP) and Beninese players strengthened their cooperation to boost intra-West African tourism. Benin's official tourism website notes that the country is recognised by international guides as a destination "to discover" for 2025. Thus, even though consolidated statistics are lacking for the full 2025 season, the indicators suggest a rebound and rising visibility.

Stakes and challenges

Despite this progress, several challenges persist. More effort is needed in tourism infrastructure, including accommodation, domestic transport, signage and rural areas that are still little developed. There is a need to strengthen the capacity to attract international and regional markets: although efforts are being made, competition is strong in West Africa. It is imperative to compile reliable statistical data: regular monitoring of tourist arrivals and revenues, updated for 2025, is still lacking. Attention must also be paid to sustainability and local value: ensuring that the benefits of tourism accrue to local communities and that sensitive sites are preserved. On the security front, some areas, notably in the north of the country, are more vulnerable, which may influence perceptions.

Medium-term outlook

If the objectives of the 2025-2029 plan are met, Benin could double its number of visitors by 2030 and significantly increase tourism's contribution to GDP. Strengthening air links, tapping into the African diaspora market, and promoting cultural and commemorative tourism (the Slave Route, the diaspora) are promising avenues. Ecotourism in areas such as Pendjari or W National Park could become a high-value niche segment. The development of upscale accommodation and quality infrastructure (resorts, international hotels) can attract higher-spending tourism.

In 2025, tourism in Benin stands at a turning point. With an ambitious strategy, historical and natural assets, and a will for regional cooperation, the country is positioning the sector as a lever for economic growth and international influence. It now remains to turn this opportunity into concrete impact: moving upmarket, quality service, sustainability and benefits for local populations. The path is laid out; the coming years will tell whether Benin can truly rise to join West Africa's must-see destinations.

Writer: Jaurès BOKO
en.4254:
Abidjan, 22 October 2025 - PRESS AFRICA - In 2025, Africa is entering a technological and scientific turning point: a proliferation of local innovations, increased cooperation and large-scale projects that are helping redefine the continent's role in the global technology race. A look at the major trends, some emblematic breakthroughs and the challenges to be met in order to turn this potential into lasting gains.

Several African countries are progressing in the Global Innovation Index (GII). The island of Mauritius leads the continental pack in 2025 with a score of 32.5, followed by Morocco (31.1) and South Africa (30.1); others, such as Nigeria (21.1), remain further behind. Moreover, the holding of forums such as the 7th African Regional Science, Technology and Innovation Forum (ARSTIF) in Kampala in April 2025 shows that the continent is emphasizing science, technology and innovation as levers of development. This framework helps explain why so many technical initiatives are emerging, often driven by local players, sometimes in international partnership.

AI, energy and research bolster African innovation in 2025

AI (artificial intelligence) is gaining ground in Africa, and not only in big cities. Startups such as Signvrse in Kenya and Rwanda are on the rise, using AI and 3D motion capture to translate sign language and make digital technology accessible to deaf people, who number more than 70 million on the continent. There is also growing attention to automated health diagnostics, using algorithms able to analyze medical images or field data to detect diseases such as tuberculosis and malaria or to predict epidemics. The stakes here are twofold: to bridge traditional infrastructure deficits while offering cutting-edge services at lower cost. Obstacles remain: access to data, digital infrastructure and talent training.

In energy, the continent, rich in natural resources but also facing the challenges of energy access and the effects of climate change, is developing innovations in next-generation solar power, with "perovskite" cells, lighter and potentially cheaper, billed as a step forward for off-grid electrification in rural areas. Battery recycling and waste management linked to renewable energy is a topic of growing importance. There are also "smart cities" and the Internet of Things (IoT) in East and Central Africa, where projects for smart traffic management, urban lighting and infrastructure sensors can be seen. These developments indicate that innovation is not isolated but connected to Africa's major challenges: electrification, rapid urbanization and climate adaptation.

The strengthening of the research and scientific training system is also under way. The Afretec Network, which brings together African technology universities, awarded more than US$2.3 million in grants in October 2025 to multi-institutional research teams in AI, robotics, cybersecurity and energy. The 2025 Innovating Education in Africa (IEA) program of the African Union Commission (AUC) selected the 10 best educational innovations for 2025, combining digital technology, STEM and inclusion. There are also initiatives such as the African Light Source, which illustrate the ambition to equip the continent with major scientific infrastructure: it has yet to materialize, but the project shows that Africa aims to move from consumer of science to producer.

The main challenges to overcome

Traditional factors such as lack of funding and infrastructure, fragile human capital, projects that fail to materialize, a non-optimized regulatory and intellectual property framework, and inequality between African countries are major challenges to be addressed.

Looking ahead, Africa has the opportunity to combine its specificities (a young population, multiplying needs, capacity for "technological leapfrogging") with scientific and technical innovation. To take full advantage, it will need to foster co-creation: innovations designed locally for local needs, then exportable; deploy incentive policies for the scale and sustainability of innovations; strengthen African scientific networks, enable research infrastructure (such as the Synchrotron project) and encourage South-South partnerships; and emphasize the ethics, inclusion and sustainability of innovations: technologies that serve everyone, not just urban centers or elites.

In 2025, Africa is no longer simply a "reservoir" for imported ideas but a player in technical and scientific innovation. The signs are there: startups, researchers, funds, infrastructure projects. The road is nonetheless strewn with challenges. The real stake will be to turn these initiatives into concrete, large-scale and lasting impact: for employment, education, health and the environment.

Writer: Jaurès BOKO
en.4237:
Lomé, 22 October 2025 - PRESS AFRICA-Togo is going through a delicate period marked by deep economic difficulties, made worse by a change of political regime which, far from bringing immediate stability, has caused budget imbalances, a slowdown in public investment and a loss of confidence among international financial partners.

A major political turning point, but at what price?

The recent change of regime in Togo (whether an anticipated democratic alternation of power or a more abrupt transition) has upset the country's institutional and economic balance. This turning point, though it carries hopes of renewed governance, has also exposed the fragility of the economic foundations on which the state rested.

From the first months after the change of power, several public projects were suspended or slowed. Ministries, in the midst of reorganisation, saw their administrative capacity reduced, affecting the management of public finances, budget disbursements and medium-term planning.

A climate of uncertainty holding back the economy

Political instability has created a wait-and-see climate among private investors. The private sector, which accounts for a large share of national economic activity, is in retreat. Several companies, notably in construction, trade and agribusiness, report late payments by the state, a drop in public orders and greater difficulty in accessing credit.

Togo's traditional financial partners, such as the IMF, the World Bank and the European Union, have adopted a cautious stance. Some aid programmes have been suspended pending a return to clear and transparent governance. The Treasury, for its part, is struggling to raise resources because of an already high debt and a sovereign rating weakened by political uncertainty.

Pressure on public and social finances

Faced with a drop in tax revenue and a rise in transition-related spending (institutional reforms, security costs, social measures to calm tensions), the budget deficit has widened. The newly elected government finds itself forced to make painful trade-offs: reducing subsidies, freezing recruitment in the civil service, or postponing major infrastructure projects.

The social consequences are tangible. Inflation, although global, is aggravated in Togo by weak local supply and the difficulty of importing amid a shortage of foreign currency. The prices of basic necessities are soaring, hitting the most vulnerable households. Social movements and strikes in the public sector reflect growing discontent.

A possible way out of the crisis?

To turn the situation around, the authorities must regain the trust of both the population and donors. This means greater transparency in the management of public finances, relaunching dialogue with economic partners, and a clear recovery strategy. Structural reforms, often deferred, will also have to be implemented to strengthen the resilience of the national economy.

In a context where political stability is still fragile, Togo's economic recovery will depend on its leaders' ability to reconcile deep reforms with emergency social measures. The population, for its part, expects the change of regime to mean a concrete improvement in living conditions, not a new era of economic uncertainty.

Writer: Jaurès S. BOKO
en.3765:
Granted a second term at the head of Fagace for having revealed it better than ever before during its existence, Dr. Nguéto Tiraïna Yambaye, the current director general, humbly accepted the offer, which he described as a "renewed mark of confidence" and is also working on developing a new strategic plan for 2026-2030. However, in an interview with Press Africa in Cotonou in early March, he maintained that he was not "a careerist," and alluded to his succession as head of the executive of the said Fund.

By Comlan Anicet TIDJO

Read the full interview

Revealed forever over the past four years by a well-born soul, affectionately referred to as the Father of Modern Fagace, the African Economic Cooperation and Guarantee Fund (ACEF) today combines modernization, innovation, notoriety, expansion, and financial stability. An interview assessing the 2021-2025 strategic plan and a harbinger of the new 2026-2030 plan.

PRESS AFRICA: Mr. Director, you need no introduction for having brought the Fagace to light. What major reforms, particularly institutional, cooperation, restructuring, and standards-related, have you implemented since your arrival at the helm of the Fund?

Nguéto Tiraïna Yambaye: Thank you for this opportunity to talk about this wonderful institution, the African Guarantee and Economic Cooperation Fund, created on February 10, 1977, in Kigali, Rwanda. Fagace is a financial institution created by the heads of state of OCAM to complete the financial ecosystem to enable African populations, African banks, and project leaders to have secure access to credit and loans. Fagace is therefore the missing link. I took office on June 1, 2020, in the midst of COVID-19, and we have tried to work rigorously and responsibly with all my staff to meet the challenge. We have developed a strategic plan that guides our vision for the next five years and is based on the modernization of the Institution.

This strategic plan has enabled us to reform the institution to bring it up to international standards; to strengthen cooperation and partnership with partner banks, similar institutions, and sister institutions, in order to develop synergy of action and pool resources to achieve Africa's underfinancing objective. The challenge is to complete the financial ecosystem so that Africa is truly financed. Africa is a potentially rich continent, but it is underfinanced. Based on macroeconomic and financial indicators, the banking rate in African economies hovers around 15%. That's for the most efficient ones, but this banking rate ranges from 2%, or even less.

As a multilateral financing and development institution, Fagace must assume its responsibilities and act to support authorities, states, the banking sector, and financial markets, and attract external financing through the private and banking sectors. We have therefore supported and developed this partnership at the global level.

The results you know indicate that Fagace is a trusted certification. We have signed cooperation agreements with multilateral institutions, rated "AAA" globally, which allow us to "reguarantee" and reinsure ourselves when we operate in fairly risky sectors. The new Fagace, through innovations I have implemented, is based on strengthening governance, rigor, responsibility, and accountability at all levels. For a good trusted certification, Fagace must inspire confidence. We are now rated "AA" by international rating agencies that recognize our efforts, internationally by Moody's. We also work with all central banks and financial market regulators that evaluate us. Several institutions evaluate us, and the International Association of Financial and Development Institutions evaluates us. And we ourselves are evaluated by our partners. We show our credentials! In strengthening governance, we have created the Independent Evaluation Office, which is an autonomous, independent body, whose members come from the four central banks of the monetary zones.

Today at Fagace, governance requires everyone, as far as they are concerned, to be rigorous and accountable. With this vision in mind, we have also created a think tank, the Fagace Institute, whose mission is to think first before deciding, because if we want to be serious, we don't act before thinking. The Institute thinks for the Director General and for the authorities, to allow us to anticipate certain actions. The Fagace Institute is managing to popularize the profession of financial guarantee, which is not yet taught in universities and colleges. We are a reformer and we work in innovation to better serve the economies of the Member States.

At what rate do you estimate the level of execution of your 2021-2025 strategic plan?

The strategic plan we developed within ourselves, which has become Fagace's guiding compass for the period 2021-2025, is very ambitious. After four years of implementation, we have exceeded our objectives by more than 300%. The secret lies in our leadership management because, since the plan was developed by ourselves; the CEO and his colleagues, the staff felt responsible for the destiny of this strategic plan. It is their strategic plan. We must create the right conditions for staff support, and therefore, we have valued the profession of Fagace's managers; the profession of guarantee by putting staff at ease. In doing so, we have achieved exceptional results. For almost five years, Fagace has delivered high-quality results to the satisfaction of the members of the Board of Governors and the Board of Directors. We have far exceeded the objectives we set for ourselves by more than 300%.

Would you like to brief us on the impacts of these results?

Indeed, when the results are positive, the impact is there! Today, the impact on the lives and working environment of staff has improved internally, as has the impact on economic operators and banks. Today, banks trust us! We work simply, but intelligently with the financial and banking markets. With the support of central banks, we are working to make the Institution useful. In 2020, the level of guarantees was 400 billion CFA francs, and as of June 30, 2024, we are at more than 1,300 billion CFA francs. The Institution has become attractive, and we receive many requests, but we do not only act on financial support in terms of guarantees. We participate as a technical assistant, as a capacity-building institution, as an institute that contributes to project structuring.

Here at Fagace, our leitmotif is that reflection must precede decisions and actions. We also conduct peer self-evaluation; that is, partners evaluate us to tell us whether the path we have taken is good or bad. Today, we were reflecting on financing rural entrepreneurs and startups. Africa is essentially an agricultural economy at 70%. If the agricultural and therefore rural economy is financed, we should not talk about famine in Africa and food self-sufficiency in Africa must be a given. Africa can even export food instead of importing it. In our philosophy, it is absolutely essential to finance the agricultural economy, which is a real economy through livestock farming, agriculture, etc. It is in the agricultural economy that there is great potential for wealth and job creation. Many young graduates from top schools are returning and want to start businesses, and we support them through the different types of guarantees that we put in place; including individual guarantees and portfolio guarantees to allow young people to have a bank account and access credit to finance the investments for their projects.

How do you see the future of Fagace in terms of projections?

Fagace is today a credible and solid institution, and my mission as Director General is to leave a positive legacy to those who will replace me. The secret to success is leadership and good governance. We are working towards this goal, and the Fagace Council of Ministers and the Board of Directors are aware that we must meet the challenge by modernizing the institution to international standards. Let the rules of the game be clear. For those who love football, if the rules of the game are not clear, there will be no football match. All stakeholders must show their credentials. Only then will we leave a Fagace with a future. The future of Fagace is promising. The new strategy we are implementing—we have already launched the “Young Professional Program.” We are rejuvenating the Fagace staff so that brilliant young people graduating from universities and prestigious schools can join this African family of experts and specialists who believe in the future of the continent and who make Fagace command the esteem and admiration of other institutions. We propose to create offices in member countries. We currently have three sub-regional representations. There is the sub-regional representation of Central Africa in the CEMAC zone in Douala, Cameroon; the sub-regional representation of East Africa in Rwanda; and the sub-regional representation of West Africa, which is in Dakar, Senegal. But, in each state, we will create offices to provide local support because the guarantee business is not very well known. Fagace should support the authorities, banks, chambers of commerce, chambers of agriculture, and project leaders so that any project leader who has good ideas can transform these ideas and support them with financing.

The paradox in Africa is that people ask themselves the question: have the banks succeeded or failed? Because in other countries, banks finance creation and ideas, but here in Africa, and particularly in French-speaking Africa, banks only finance development. We only finance what exists. We want to break with this because it's not the quantity of money that will make a success, but the quality of the ideas and the competence of the actors. Fagace has a good future, and I believe in humble conscience that I will leave a good legacy to the future generation for the prosperity of Africa.

Your Excellency, the member countries have renewed their confidence in you. In what frame of mind are you approaching this second term?

The Board of Governors renewed my mandate early in light of past results, but it is with humility that I begin this second term. I tell myself that I am not a careerist! I want to be useful to the continent: my country is Africa and Chad is my village! I have served the continent in all capacities and it was with pleasure that I accepted the position of Director General of Fagace and this second term entrusted to me is a mark of confidence. It is therefore up to me to continue to modernize the Institution; to bring it up to international standards; to work above all to restructure it and train human resources. We must be competitive at the global level.

We are not self-conscious, and my colleagues are fortunate to have a Director General with extensive experience; proven expertise at the global level, and who, through his commitment to his continent, has come back down to earth to be more useful. The Board of Governors has renewed my mandate; I must develop a new strategic plan for the period 2026-2030. We are already working on it, and we will do better than the first strategic plan. So, the second strategic plan for the period 2026-2030 is underway with the same team and the contribution of new states that are in the process of joining. Our capital has increased from 300 billion to 500 billion CFA francs. We have several English-speaking and Portuguese-speaking states that will join, and non-state institutions that are also interested in what we are doing. Our role is to continue supporting the continent and supporting accelerated development financing.

You couldn't achieve these feats without a secret?

The secret is that we took our work seriously. The new guidelines given to me during my recruitment were rigorously implemented. This strategic plan focuses on strengthening the institution and also focuses on its modernization. We have met the challenge entrusted to us by the Board of Governors to become a modern pan-African institution aligned with international standards. The results of the modernization we have achieved are convincing. For the past five years, Fagace has been making positive and growing profits. The rating agencies and central banks that evaluate us every six months through the Independent Evaluation Office are satisfied and encourage us to do better. We cannot assume that we have already succeeded in modernizing Fagace. There are still many challenges to enable potentially very wealthy African economies to realize their potential by providing substantial financing and playing our role in the financing and development mechanism of the African continent. If some people in public opinion think that I am the father of modern Fagace, they are somewhat right and it is because I have applied the governors' guidelines so that Fagace becomes a modern and innovative institution serving the accelerated financing of African economies.

What will be the essence of the next strategic plan?

The current strategic plan will be completed in 2025. The Fagace teams will get to work to prepare a new strategic plan, still focused on the modernization and efficiency of the institution. The next strategic plan will be a continuation of the current plan, which was already a success. But, I told my colleagues, the challenge is enormous. We must be a useful institution, not only for our staff, but for the entire continent. We anticipate new memberships from other states, about ten. There are also non-state institutions that want to join Fagace. All of this must be completed by 2025 and integrated into the new 2026-2030 vision.

What about governance mode?

Fagace must be a model! Fagace must be an example! As a general manager, I must govern by example, and the staff's support is reassuring. My management is participatory; that is, the work must be shared. As a general manager, I don't work alone in my little corner. We share the work; we share the joys, and we also share the difficulties together. Fagace's management framework has been strengthened so that participatory management is the rule at Fagace.

You have received a flurry of honorary distinctions; are they a source of motivation?

These distinctions and decorations encourage me to be an exemplary leader. The challenge is the reputation of the institution I represent and lead. These honorary distinctions and decorations further galvanize me.

What is your final word?

I would first like to sincerely thank the entire Fagace staff for their commitment, the new social contract, and their sacrifice. My staff works an average of 60 hours a week without asking for anything in return. This means that it is their Fagace first and foremost; they are personal and must be exemplary. Our motto is also strengthening governance. I would also like to thank our partners in the national and international press in the countries that support us. It is thanks to the press that Fagace continues to be known in the Member States and globally. Today, Fagace's commitment is to work in both languages: English and French. This is an innovation that allows us to get our message across the world. We have partners at the global, African, and national levels who support us. We are also not only a financing institution, but also a consulting institution, and we provide our technical assistance and expertise. The financial engineering demonstrated by Fagace is put at the service of states, banks, and the private sector. Today, building the capacity of our partners is also part of our responsibilities. We are doing this, and we believe that by 2025, our partners will regularly provide us with feedback so that we can be of service to them. Fagace is at the service of states and economies, not the other way around. We are doing our bit so that tomorrow, the new generation that will take over Fagace will be able to continue what we have sown.

As Akinwumi Adesina's term as President of the African Development Bank (ADF) draws to a close, it's time to take stock. And what a record it is! Elected in 2015 and re-elected in 2020, the Nigerian economist has made his mark with bold initiatives and tangible results that have strengthened the ADF's role as a driving force for economic development in Africa.

By Koffi Didi HOUNNOU

Under his leadership, the ADF has deployed ambitious strategies, notably through the ‘High 5’, five major priorities aimed at transforming the continent: Light up and electrify Africa, with massive investments in renewable energy and access to electricity for millions of Africans; Feed Africa, by financing innovative agricultural projects and supporting farmers to boost food security; Industrialising Africa, by facilitating access to capital for local industries and promoting the structural transformation of African economies; Integrating Africa, with strategic investments in transport and trade infrastructure; Improving the quality of life of African populations, by developing projects to provide access to water, education and health. Thanks to these initiatives, significant progress has been made. More than 18 million people have had access to electricity, 141 million have benefited from improved agricultural technologies, 15 million have been able to access financing for entrepreneurship, and 105 million have benefited from modern transport infrastructures. These achievements are to be applauded for their impact on growth indicators and the development of human capital.

A resilient and visionary management approach

By Koffi DidBeyond the figures, Akinwumi Adesina has successfully navigated a global context marked by the Covid-19 pandemic and economic crises. The ADF distinguished itself by its responsiveness in setting up a $10 billion fund to support African economies in the face of the health crisis. The institution also successfully raised a $3 billion social Eurobond, the largest ever issued by a multilateral institution to combat the pandemic. In addition, under his tenure, the ADF maintained its triple A rating from the rating agencies, testifying to its financial solidity and the confidence of donors. Under his leadership, the Bank's capital has grown significantly, from $201 billion in 2019 to $318 billion. This increase has strengthened the ADF's capacity to finance development projects across the continent. Over the past eight years, the ADF has invested 50 billion dollars in infrastructure, covering key sectors such as energy, transport and water, helping to improve connectivity and quality of life in Africa. Under Akinwumi Adesina, the ADF has effectively supported agriculture and agro-industrial transformation. It is hard to overlook the many pleas for a fair global financial architecture. Adesina has been a fervent advocate of reforming the global financial architecture to better meet Africa's needs. He has proposed solutions to increase available financing, simplify access to climate funds and improve the restructuring of African debt.

A legacy to be preserved and strengthened

Akinwumi Adesina leaves behind a stronger, more influential ADF, more committed to the continent's development. His successor will have the onerous task of maintaining this momentum and pursuing the reforms already underway. Africa is at a decisive turning point, where consolidating the gains made is essential to accelerate the continent's economic emergence. The challenges remain numerous: accelerating the energy transition, strengthening food self-sufficiency, attracting more private investment and deepening regional integration. But thanks to the impetus provided by Adesina, the ADF now has a solid base from which to meet these challenges successfully. Now is not the time to change course, but to step up our efforts. The next President of the ADF must be a builder of continuity, a visionary capable of capitalising on the progress made. Because more than ever, Africa needs a strong, proactive institution to realise its potential.

In Guinea, efforts to consolidate peace and promote dialogue are taking on new forms. At the initiative of journalists and the “Arbre à Palabre” association, Dr Sékou Kouréissy Condé, a key figure in the quest for peace in Guinea, took part in a constructive debate on the state of national dialogue.

By Koffi Didi HOUNNOU

The meeting, marked by intense and fruitful exchanges, provided an opportunity to discuss the country's current situation in depth. It also brought to light a collective determination to give priority to dialogue and consensus as the essential means of guaranteeing the national interest. At the end of the discussions, Dr Sékou Kouréissy Condé underlined the importance of this approach, which testifies to the increased commitment of the media and civil society organizations in the search for peaceful solutions. “Dialogue and consensus-building remain the two options to be considered in the national interest”, he asserted. This initiative, led by actors often perceived as mere observers, reflects a new dynamic in which all components of Guinean society are mobilizing to build a harmonious future. In a context where political and social tensions persist, this type of platform could well represent a model to follow in strengthening national cohesion.

A life of peace and dialogue

A key figure on the Guinean political and social scene, Dr Sékou Kouréissy Condé has established himself over the years as a tireless artisan of peace. A man of dialogue, he embodies balanced mediation and an unwavering determination to build bridges between different political factions, communities and generations. An executive with a wealth of experience and a rich political background, this unique figure wears many hats, and is an unrivalled mediator whose reputation crosses borders. A former minister and president of the Aréna party, Dr Condé has combined institutional experience and proximity to citizens throughout his career. His university training, his expertise in sociology and political science, and his commitment in the field make him a credible interlocutor respected by all parties.

Continuous commitment and availability

Dr Sékou Kouréissy Condé has always placed dialogue at the heart of his actions. In a country marked by recurrent ethnic, social and political tensions, he advocates an inclusive approach, favoring listening, understanding and compromise. “Dialogue is the only way to preserve national unity”, he often repeats. This conviction has led him to intervene in numerous crises, playing a key role in de-escalating conflicts. Faced with the challenges facing Guinea, Dr Condé campaigns for peace not as a mere aspiration, but as a concrete, structured project. As a political player and well-informed citizen, he works to promote a culture of peace by bringing together players from different backgrounds to discuss national issues freely. Through this platform, he encourages a genuine “participatory democracy” where every voice counts. A fight for social and political peace in Guinea.

Recognised human and professional qualities

What sets Dr Sékou Kouréissy Condé apart is above all his humanism. A man of consensus, he favors open and sincere dialogue, without taking sides. His natural charisma, eloquence and ability to ease tensions have earned him the respect of political leaders and grassroots citizens alike. His pragmatic approach, combined with a deep understanding of socio-political dynamics, enable him to propose realistic solutions tailored to the country's needs. For Dr Condé, peace requires national reconciliation based on justice, equity and transparency. He insists on the need to take into account the wounds of the past while building a common future. “Peace is not a gift, it's a constant effort that requires everyone's contribution”, he asserts as a plea for national reconciliation.

A model for future generations

Beyond his role as a public man, Dr Sékou Kouréissy Condé strives to inspire younger generations. He calls on them to reject violence and embrace the values of tolerance and unity. His vision of a united, prosperous and peaceful Guinea resonates particularly in a context where divisions often threaten the country's stability. In short, Dr Sékou Kouréissy Condé embodies the hope of a Guinea reconciled with itself. His fight for peace, his dedication to dialogue and his faith in the ability of Guineans to overcome their differences make him a key player in building a harmonious future for the country.

Sociology of agreement: a concept that is gaining ground

“In a global context marked by growing social tensions, the sociology of understanding is emerging as an essential discipline for understanding and promoting social cohesion”, argues Dr Sékou Kouréissy Condé, a leading mediator, political player, conscientious objector and informed citizen of Guinean politics. Often referred to as the sociology of dialogue, cooperation or reconciliation, this branch of the social sciences is concerned with the processes and mechanisms by which individuals and human groups manage to find common ground, build harmonious relationships and work together to achieve common goals.

As a science at the service of unity, the sociology of understanding is not limited to the observation of conflicts and tensions. It proposes concrete tools for overcoming them, by promoting dialogue, mutual understanding and cooperation. In a Guinean society marked by political and social challenges, this discipline can play a key role in strengthening national unity and promoting inclusive development. For Dr Sékou Kouréissy Condé, understanding cannot be decreed: it has to be built patiently, thanks to the willingness of social and political players to overcome their differences for the benefit of a collective interest. By valuing local traditions of palaver and mediation, while drawing inspiration from modern approaches to conflict management, the sociology of understanding offers a promising path to building a harmonious future.

A call for collective patriotism

Guinea, with its rich cultural and ethnic diversity, has everything to gain by investing in the promotion of understanding. This project, far from being a task for the elite alone, concerns every citizen. “The future of our nation depends on our ability to work together, beyond our differences”, says Dr Condé. In short, the sociology of understanding embodies a veritable compass for guiding Guinea towards a future marked by peace, solidarity and shared prosperity. A noble goal, but above all a patriotic duty.
